## 18. NCSC-NL, Talos & Mandiant — China-Nexus APT: FortiOS SSL-VPN & COATHANGER Persistent RAT
- **Scenario ID:** `talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/talos-fortinet-coathanger-apt
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-21762 (9.6 CRITICAL), CVE-2022-42475 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** COATHANGER Espionage Actor (Volt/Red Menshen Overlap), UNC3886 & Perimeter Appliance Actors
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker sends an HTTPS request to the FortiGate VPN login gate with a falsified Content-Length label, causing the sslvpnd gatekeeper to pour extra bytes past the end of its memory bucket (Heap Overflow) and overwrite its own instruction pointer. The attacker sends a specially crafted HTTPS request with a manipulated Content-Length header or encrypted parameter (enc) to the FortiGate SSL-VPN web endpoint (/remote/logincheck or /remote/hostcheck_validate, public VPN login pages reachable from the internet without prior authentication). This triggers a heap-based buffer overflow inside the sslvpnd daemon (writing attacker-controlled bytes past the end of the allocated heap buffer to overwrite adjacent function pointers in RAM and hijack the CPU into running the attacker’s code). In FortiOS, sslvpnd and almost all system utilities are compiled into a single monolithic multi-call binary (/bin/init). By chaining Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) gadgets inside that binary, exploiting sslvpnd gives the attacker immediate code execution inside the underlying Linux OS of the firewall. In the documented FortiOS Crashlog exchange from China-Nexus APT C2 to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK CVE-2024-21762 (confirming that the SSLVPND SIGSEGV request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 COATHANGER PRELOAD.SO ROOTKIT & SMARTCTL HOOK). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SSLVPND SIGSEGV / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-21762) from Node ① (#1 China-Nexus APT C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Once inside, COATHANGER places a filter lens (preload.so) in /etc/ld.so.preload. Whenever any program on the firewall asks Linux "What files are in /data2?" or "What processes are running?", the filter lens intercepts the answer and deletes COATHANGER’s name before showing the list. COATHANGER stores its backdoor files inside the persistent /data2/ partition and writes the path of its malicious shared library (preload.so) into /etc/ld.so.preload (a special Linux dynamic-linker configuration file that forces every single program launched on the system to load preload.so before the standard C library libc.so). Because preload.so is loaded first, it intercepts file-listing and process-listing calls (removing COATHANGER’s files and PIDs from the results so an admin inspecting the firewall sees nothing unusual). By hooking user-space libc functions like readdir(), open(), and stat() via /etc/ld.so.preload, whenever an administrator runs a diagnostic CLI command on the FortiGate, the hooked library filters out any path containing the implant’s directory before returning the output to the terminal. In the documented NCSC-NL YARA Match exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd), FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd) responds with ALERT 36 KB ELF (confirming that the COATHANGER ROOTKIT request succeeded on FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 MASQUERADED HTTPSD BEACON & VPN CREDENTIAL THEFT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ COATHANGER ROOTKIT / ⇠#2 ALERT 36 KB ELF) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Even if the IT team installs a brand-new FortiOS firmware update, COATHANGER has already tucked a backup copy of itself inside the emergency kernel unpacker (flatkc) so that as soon as the newly updated firewall reboots, it re-infects itself on startup. Normally, rebooting a FortiGate or installing a FortiOS firmware update wipes the temporary root filesystem in RAM and loads a clean image. To survive both reboots and firmware updates, COATHANGER replaces /bin/smartctl and hooks the flatkc boot binary (the low-level FortiOS unpacker that initializes the filesystem whenever the appliance boots up, causing the firewall to automatically copy the hidden backdoor from the persistent /data2 flash partition back into the freshly updated system on startup). Because standard firmware upgrades replace the main rootfs image but preserve persistent flash partitions like /data2 alongside hooked boot components, simply installing a FortiOS patch without wiping and reformatting the appliance leaves COATHANGER active. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ FORTIGATE EGRESS C2 / ⇠#3 ALERT TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 FortiGate NGFW (sslvpnd)) to Node ④ (#4 COATHANGER (preload.so & smartctl)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SOC NDR & Firmware Auditor).

## 19. F5 Security & Mandiant — F5 BIG-IP TMUI AJP Request Smuggling to Root RCE

- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-46747 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** UNC5174 & Perimeter Appliance Exploiters, Initial Access Brokers Targeting Load Balancers
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker sends a request to a public login helper page (/tmui/Control/jspmap/tmui/locallb/workspace/tmshCmd.jsp) with a precisely sized HTTP header that overflows the internal AJP pneumatic tube packet, sneaking a hidden second AJP message (REMOTE_USER=admin) right behind it. By carefully sizing the HTTP headers and body, mod_proxy_ajp on the front-end Apache server miscalculates the binary AJP packet boundary and forwards the attacker’s raw payload bytes as a brand-new, second AJP request (starting with the AJP magic bytes 0x12 0x34) to the back-end Tomcat server on port 8009, with the internal AJP header attribute SC_A_REMOTE_USER set to "admin" (spoofing a fully authenticated administrator session because Tomcat blindly trusts whichever username the front-end Apache proxy puts in SC_A_REMOTE_USER). In a two-tier Apache + Tomcat AJP architecture, Tomcat does not re-verify passwords; it assumes the front-end Apache server already checked the user’s login before setting SC_A_REMOTE_USER. Smuggling a raw second AJP frame inside the socket stream lets an unauthenticated attacker inject SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin directly into Tomcat. In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-46747 exchange from Threat Actor (AJP Smuggler) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT HTTP 200 (confirming that the AJP SMUGGLING POST request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 ROGUE ADMIN ACCOUNT CREATION VIA TMSHCMD.JSP). When Tomcat processes the smuggled /tmui/Control/form request with SC_A_REMOTE_USER=admin, it communicates with the BIG-IP master control daemon (mcpd) to write the new administrator account into /config/bigip_user.conf. (abusing the Traffic Management Shell’s built-in "/util bash" utility to break out of the restricted appliance CLI into an unrestricted Linux root shell). ## 20. Splunk STRT & Mandiant — Ivanti Connect Secure (UNC5221): Auth Bypass, RCE & ZIPLINE Backdoor
- **Scenario ID:** `splunk-ivanti-connect-secure`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/splunk-ivanti-connect-secure
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-21887 (9.1 CRITICAL), CVE-2023-46805 (8.2 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** UNC5221 / UTA0178, UNC5325 & Post-Disclosure Clusters
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The outer door guard (web daemon) has a checklist that says: "Anyone walking down the /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/ hallway does not need to be logged in yet." The attacker starts down that hallway, but immediately takes two ../../ steps backward into the restricted /license/keys-status/ room, slipping right past the outer guard. In Ivanti Connect Secure, the outer web gatekeeper checks whether a requested URL starts with a public prefix like /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/ (an endpoint that must be reachable before login so users who lost their phone can submit a backup 2FA code). By requesting /api/v1/totp/user-backup-code/../../license/keys-status/, the outer gatekeeper sees the allowed prefix and waves the request through without asking for a password, while the internal Python router resolves the "../../" path traversal and hands the request straight to the restricted admin-only /api/v1/license/keys-status/ endpoint. Because the authentication filter checked the raw un-normalized URI prefix (startswith("/api/v1/totp/user-backup-code")) before the backend web framework normalized "../" segments (CVE-2023-46805), any unauthenticated internet client can reach any internal REST API endpoint on the VPN appliance. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CVE-2024-21887 RCE / ⇠#1 ALERT HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 UNC5221 / UTA0178 Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now standing at the restricted /license/keys-status/ counter without ever logging in, the attacker writes ;python -c ... # in the node-name field. The Python clerk pastes that string straight into a popen() shell command and runs it as root. Once the path-traversal request reaches /api/v1/license/keys-status/;python%20-c%20..., the backend Python handler takes the URL parameter and passes it directly into subprocess.Popen(..., shell=True) without input sanitization (CVE-2024-21887, an OS command injection flaw where untrusted URL characters are interpreted as live Linux shell commands). Inside that string, the semicolon (; which in Bash/sh terminates the legitimate license-check command and immediately executes the attacker’s python -c payload right behind it) runs the attacker’s code with full root privileges. Why did the attacker chain two CVEs? Because CVE-2024-21887 (command injection in keys-status) normally required an administrator login, and CVE-2023-46805 (path traversal) only bypassed authentication without running code. Combining both inside a single HTTP URL turns them into a 1-packet unauthenticated root RCE. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ZIPLINE ELF HOOK / ⇠#2 ALERT 72 KB ELF) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Ivanti Connect Secure VPN), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): To stay inside permanently, the attacker remounts the read-only floor tiles as writable, slips the WIREFIRE webshell into visits.py, plants the ZIPLINE LD_PRELOAD rootkit in libsecure.so, and modifies the login page JavaScript (WARPWIRE) to steal every employee’s plaintext VPN password as they log in. Synthesizing Volexity (UTA0178) and Mandiant (UNC5221) findings, with root access on the VPN appliance the attacker runs mount -o remount,rw / (temporarily unlocking the appliance’s read-only system partition so built-in files can be edited) and deploys a multi-layered malware suite: (1) Volexity’s WIREFIRE Python webshell injected directly inside visits.py (modifying an already-existing API file so basic file-count checks do not spot an extra file) and WARPWIRE JavaScript credential harvester injected into the VPN login page to steal plaintext Active Directory passwords; plus (2) Mandiant’s ZIPLINE passive backdoor loaded via LD_PRELOAD inside libsecure.so (intercepting accept() network calls inside the legitimate Ivanti web daemon). As Mandiant UNC5221 documented, the threat actor also patches ComponentIntegrity.pm (so Ivanti’s built-in Integrity Checker Tool reports "0 modified files" when an admin runs an internal self-check, which is why CISA ED 24-01 mandated running the external offline ICT snapshot tool). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DSLOG.PM CRED STEAL / ⇠#3 ACK Cred Harvest) from Node ③ (#3 Ivanti Connect Secure VPN) to Node ④ (#4 ZIPLINE Passive Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).

## 21. Splunk STRT, Mandiant & CISA — Citrix Bleed: NetScaler OOB Memory Leak & NSC_AAAC Hijack
- **Scenario ID:** `splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/splunk-citrix-bleed-session-hijack
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-4966 (9.4 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** LockBit 3.0 Affiliates (Citrix Bleed Campaign), Medusa & Rhysida Ransomware Groups
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker asks the public OpenID info desk (/oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration) for its standard welcome sheet while supplying a 24,576-byte Host name. Because snprintf() reports how many bytes it wanted to write (147 KB) rather than the size of the 131 KB paper sheet, the server sends back 16 KB of raw adjacent RAM right after the welcome sheet. As reverse-engineered by Assetnote, the attacker sends an unauthenticated HTTPS GET request to /oauth/idp/.well-known/openid-configuration (a public discovery page on the Citrix NetScaler Gateway whose ns_aaa_oauthrp_send_openid_config function inserts the caller’s HTTP Host header into six JSON URL fields: issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, jwks_uri, userinfo_endpoint, and end_session_endpoint). By sending a 24,576-byte Host header, the 6 copies total ~147 KB, exceeding the server’s 131,072-byte (0x20000) stack response buffer. Because C’s snprintf() function returns how many bytes it wanted to write (147 KB) rather than how many bytes actually fit in the 128 KB buffer, NetScaler’s SSL_write transmits the 128 KB buffer PLUS ~16 KB of raw adjacent nsppe memory straight back to the attacker. In the C standard library, snprintf(buf, size, fmt...) stops writing at size bytes to prevent a crash, but returns the theoretical total length of the formatted string. Passing that unchecked return value directly to the HTTP socket writer causes an out-of-bounds memory over-read (CVE-2023-4966) from the NetScaler packet engine (nsppe). In the documented Suricata CVE-2023-4966 exchange from Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT 148 KB Leak (confirming that the CITRIX BLEED GET request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 NSC_AAAC SESSION COOKIE EXTRACTION & MFA BYPASS). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CITRIX BLEED GET / ⇠#1 ALERT 148 KB Leak) from Node ① (#1 Threat Actor (LockBit / UNC)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Scanning the accidentally photocopied desk pages, the attacker spots a 65-digit hexadecimal VIP wristband (NSC_AAAC) belonging to an administrator who is currently logged in. Clipping that wristband onto their own browser lets the attacker step straight into the admin’s active Citrix Virtual Desktop without any password or MFA prompt. Scanning the leaked raw memory dump with a regular expression ([0-9a-f]{32,65}), the attacker extracts a 65-character hexadecimal string: a live NSC_AAAC session cookie (the master authentication token stored in nsppe memory for a user who has already logged in and passed Multi-Factor Authentication). By pasting Cookie: NSC_AAAC=<leaked_token> into their own browser, the attacker hijacks the administrator’s active Citrix session (bypassing both the password screen and MFA completely). Because the NSC_AAAC cookie represents an active server-side AAA session in NetScaler memory, even patching the appliance or resetting the victim’s Active Directory password does not kick the attacker out unless the administrator explicitly flushes active sessions on the appliance via kill aaa session -all and kill icaconnection -all. In the documented NetScaler SSLVPN Log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway, Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway responds with RESP IP Mismatch (confirming that the REPLAY NSC_AAAC request succeeded on Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 CITRIX ICA VDI LAUNCH & INTERNAL AD RECONNAISSANCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ REPLAY NSC_AAAC / ⇠#2 RESP IP Mismatch) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now sitting at the administrator’s virtual desk inside the building, the attacker uses the internal intercom (DCOM MMC20.Application over port 135) to command neighboring Windows servers to run commands on their behalf. Inside the hijacked Citrix Virtual Desktop (VDI) session, the attacker runs Active Directory discovery tools (adfind / SoftPerfect netscan), deploys remote management tunnels (AnyDesk / eHorus), and uses Distributed COM (DCOM, invoking the MMC20.Application COM object over RPC port 135, which instructs a remote Windows server to silently launch mmc.exe -Embedding and execute commands via Document.ActiveView.ExecuteShellCommand without creating a noisy new Windows service). Unlike PsExec or sc.exe (which register a new Windows Service and trigger System EventID 7045 on the target server), lateral movement via DCOM MMC20.Application abuses an already-registered Microsoft COM class over TCP/135. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ VDI POWERSHELL RECON / ⇠#3 ACK PID 5310) from Node ③ (#3 Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway) to Node ④ (#4 Hijacked NSC_AAAC Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk Enterprise Security (STRT)).

## 22. Kaspersky GReAT — Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB
- **Scenario ID:** `kaspersky-operation-triangulation`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/kaspersky-operation-triangulation
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-38606 (8.8 HIGH), CVE-2023-41990 (7.8 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Operation Triangulation Threat Actor, Zero-Click Mobile Surveillance Operators
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): An invisible iMessage arrives while the phone is sitting untouched on a table. As the background mail-preview clerk (IMAgent) tries to render a custom font inside the attachment, an obsolete 1990s font command (ADJUST) tricks the clerk into writing outside the page boundary. The target iPhone receives an iMessage containing a disguised PDF/archive attachment with an embedded TrueType font. Even while the phone is locked in a pocket, the background daemon IMAgent (the iOS process that automatically pre-processes incoming iMessage attachments before showing a notification) parses the font using libFontParser.dylib. Inside the font, an obsolete 1990s TrueType bytecode instruction named ADJUST (opcode 0x8F/0x90, CVE-2023-41990) triggers an out-of-bounds memory write, giving the attacker instant code execution inside IMAgent with zero user clicks ("Zero-Click"). TrueType fonts are not just static shapes; they contain a Turing-complete virtual machine (font hinting bytecode) designed in the early 1990s. Abusing the legacy ADJUST instruction corrupts the C++ vtable on the heap inside IMAgent before any UI notification is ever rendered. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IMTRANSFERAGENT C2 / ⇠#1 RESP TLS 1.3) from Node ① (#1 Triangulation Validator & C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Even after taking over the kernel, the chip’s hardware Page Protection Layer (PPL) blocks any software from altering protected memory pages. So the exploit talks directly to an undocumented hardware controller on the Apple Silicon die (0x206040000) and commands its hardware DMA engine to overwrite the protected RAM directly, going completely around the CPU’s software guard. Even after escalating into the iOS kernel, Apple Silicon chips enforce a hardware-backed Page Protection Layer (PPL, which blocks even the operating system kernel itself from modifying protected user-signing tables or injecting unsigned code). To bypass PPL, the exploit writes directly to undocumented physical Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers at address 0x206040000 (CVE-2023-38606, an unmapped hardware debugging/DMA block built into the Apple A12–A16 System-on-Chip). By commanding this hardware DMA engine to write directly to physical RAM, the attacker overwrites PPL-protected kernel memory completely outside the CPU’s security checks. Because the CPU’s MMU/PPL checks only apply to memory writes executed by the CPU cores themselves, instructing an on-chip peripheral DMA engine via MMIO registers to write to physical memory bypasses PPL page-table write protection. In the documented CVE-2023-38606 MMIO exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC), IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) responds with ALERT Ring-0 / PPL (confirming that the MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS request succeeded on IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS / ⇠#2 ALERT Ring-0 / PPL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Once inside the vault, the exploit shreds the incoming iMessage from sms.db so the user never sees a trace, and runs the TriangleDB spyware strictly in volatile RAM, leaving behind only subtle water-meter readings (DataUsage.sqlite network byte counters) that forensic investigators can spot. With full kernel privileges, the exploit first deletes the triggering iMessage record from sms.db and attachment caches (so the victim never sees an unread message and forensic investigators cannot extract the exploit file from the phone), and then launches the TriangleDB spyware implant strictly in volatile RAM (meaning zero implant files are written to flash storage; if the phone is rebooted, the implant vanishes completely to avoid capture). Even though TriangleDB deletes its iMessage entry and runs only in RAM, iOS automatically records how many bytes of cellular/Wi-Fi data each process uses inside DataUsage.sqlite, leaving orphaned network-usage rows and timestamp gaps that Kaspersky’s triangle_check forensic tool uses to prove infection. In the documented Mach-O TriangleDB exchange from IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) to XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers, XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers responds with ALERT 220 KB Mach-O (confirming that the LOAD TRIANGLEDB request succeeded on XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT, Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ LOAD TRIANGLEDB / ⇠#3 ALERT 220 KB Mach-O) from Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)) to Node ④ (#4 XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).

## 23. Kaspersky GReAT — ToddyCat APT: ESET Scanner DLL Proxying (CVE-2024-11859) & TCESB Loader
- **Scenario ID:** `kaspersky-toddycat-eset-dll`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/kaspersky-toddycat-eset-dll
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-11859 (6.7 MEDIUM (Abused for Stealth APT Execution))
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** ToddyCat APT, UNC-Exchange-Samurai Clusters
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker places a real, digitally signed ESET scanner (ecls.exe) and a forged helper library (version.dll) in the same folder (C:\ProgramData\ESET\). Because of CVE-2024-11859, the moment ecls.exe starts, it grabs the version.dll sitting right next to it instead of the real Windows System32\version.dll. The attacker drops a standalone, validly signed copy of ESET Command Line Scanner (ecls.exe, an authentic antivirus utility whose valid digital signature passes Windows AppLocker and antivirus file checks) into a writable folder like C:\ProgramData\ESET\ right next to a malicious library named version.dll. Because of CVE-2024-11859 (where ecls.exe did not restrict its DLL load path to System32), the moment ecls.exe starts, Windows loads the attacker’s version.dll from C:\ProgramData\ESET\ before checking C:\Windows\System32\version.dll. Unlike KnownDLLs (such as kernel32.dll or ntdll.dll, which Windows forces every program to load exclusively from System32), version.dll is not on the Default KnownDLLs list, so any executable that imports version.dll without specifying LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 will load a local version.dll from its own folder first. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HIJACK VERSION.DLL / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-11859) from Node ① (#1 ToddyCat C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): If the rigged version.dll didn’t know how to answer normal version-check questions, ecls.exe would crash immediately. So the rigged DLL acts as a middleman ("Export Proxying"): it forwards every real question to C:\Windows\System32\version.dll while quietly decrypting ToddyCat’s TCESB backdoor in the background. If the attacker’s version.dll failed to answer the normal version-check functions that ecls.exe calls on startup (like GetFileVersionInfoW), ecls.exe would crash immediately with an error popup. To prevent a crash, the malicious version.dll uses DLL Export Proxying (forwarding every normal API call straight through to the real C:\Windows\System32\version.dll so ecls.exe runs smoothly), while its background thread reads an encrypted file from disk and decrypts ToddyCat’s TCESB backdoor directly into RAM. By adding linker export forwarders in the malicious DLL’s Export Address Table (pointing functions like GetFileVersionInfoW to C:\Windows\System32\version.GetFileVersionInfoW), the host program continues to work normally while the attacker’s decrypted shellcode runs in the same process memory. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ TCESB UNPACK RAM / ⇠#2 ALERT 184 KB RWX) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The malware now phones home from inside the signed ecls.exe process. However, defenders catch the trick because ecls.exe is an offline command-line file scanner, it has zero reason to ever open an outbound HTTPS connection to the internet! Running inside the memory space of the signed ecls.exe process (so process lists show a legitimate ESET security scanner), the decrypted TCESB backdoor opens an encrypted HTTPS tunnel on TCP port 443 to ToddyCat’s command-and-control server to harvest domain credentials and browser cookies. Why is this still detectable by defenders? Because ecls.exe is a standalone, offline on-demand file scanner that never connects to the internet during normal operation, meaning any Sysmon EventID 3 (NetworkConnect) log showing ecls.exe opening an outbound TCP/443 socket is an immediate indicator of compromise. In the documented Sysmon EID 3 exchange from ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner) to version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM, version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM responds with ACK TLS 1.3 (confirming that the ECLS.EXE C2 BEACON request succeeded on version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT, ToddyCat APT: ESET Scanner DLL Proxying (CVE-2024-11859) & TCESB Loader). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ECLS.EXE C2 BEACON / ⇠#3 ACK TLS 1.3) from Node ③ (#3 ecls.exe (Signed ESET Scanner)) to Node ④ (#4 version.dll Proxy & TCESB RAM), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky Anti-Targeted Attack).

## 24. Kaspersky, Microsoft & Avast — Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet): appid.sys Zero-Day & FUDModule Rootkit
- **Scenario ID:** `kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/kaspersky-lazarus-byovd-fudmodule
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-21338 (7.8 HIGH (Local Kernel 0-Day))
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet / Labyrinth Chollima), Andariel & BlueNoroff Subgroups
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Instead of sneaking an untrusted third-party driver file onto the disk, the attacker simply walks up to the office door of Windows’ own pre-installed AppLocker driver (\Device\AppId / appid.sys) using a LOCAL SERVICE badge. Because modern Windows blocks untrusted kernel drivers via Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) and Microsoft’s Vulnerable Driver Blocklist, the attacker does not drop any third-party .sys file onto the disk. Instead, they elevate a user-mode process to LOCAL SERVICE privileges (required because \Device\AppId’s access control list only lets LOCAL SERVICE, rather than standard Administrators, open a communication handle to it) and open a device handle to Windows’ own built-in AppLocker driver: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\appid.sys. Abusing a pre-installed inbox Windows driver (appid.sys, Living off the Land in the Kernel) completely sidesteps HVCI / Vulnerable Driver Blocklist checks because appid.sys is an official part of the Windows operating system. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ APPID.SYS IOCTL 0x22A018 / ⇠#1 RET PreviousMode=0) from Node ① (#1 Lazarus (Diamond Sleet) C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Every thread in Windows wears a tag (KTHREAD.PreviousMode) that says 1 (User Mode: check all permissions) or 0 (Kernel Mode: trust everything). By passing a forged pointer in IOCTL 0x22A018, FudModule tricks appid.sys into reaching over and flipping the attacker thread’s tag from 1 to 0. FudModule calls DeviceIoControl with control code IOCTL 0x22A018 (which invokes the internal function AipSmartHashImageFile inside appid.sys) and passes a crafted structure containing a spoofed function/object pointer (CVE-2024-21338). This tricks the kernel driver into decrementing the attacker thread’s KTHREAD.PreviousMode byte in kernel memory from 1 (UserMode, where Windows blocks the thread from touching kernel RAM) to 0 (KernelMode, telling the Windows kernel to treat every subsequent NtReadVirtualMemory and NtWriteVirtualMemory call from this thread as if it came from the kernel itself, granting unlimited Ring-0 memory read/write). When a thread calls NtWriteVirtualMemory, the kernel checks KTHREAD->PreviousMode: if it is 1 (UserMode), the kernel rejects any target address above 0x7FFFFFFEFFFF (protecting kernel space). Once CVE-2024-21338 flips PreviousMode to 0 (KernelMode), the thread can read and overwrite any address in the Windows kernel directly from user mode. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ BLIND SYSMON & ETW-TI / ⇠#2 ALERT EDR Blinded) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 appid.sys (AppLocker Driver)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): If a burglar shoots out a security camera, the guard desk immediately sees a "CAMERA OFFLINE" alarm. Instead, FudModule leaves the EDR security program running happily so its green status light stays on, while erasing its phone number from the kernel’s notification list (PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine) so the kernel never tells the EDR about new malware. Instead of killing the endpoint’s EDR security service (which would immediately set off a "Sensor Offline" alarm on the SOC dashboard), FudModule uses its new kernel read/write access (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation, DKOM) to overwrite the kernel’s PspCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, PspCreateThreadNotifyRoutine, and ObRegisterCallbacks arrays with zeroes (erasing the kernel notification hooks that tell the EDR whenever a new process or thread starts) and disables EtwThreatIntProvRegHandle (shutting off Microsoft’s Kernel Threat-Intelligence telemetry feed so the EDR agent stays running with a green status light, but is completely blind and deaf). By surgically zeroing out the callback pointers registered by the security vendor’s kernel driver (.sys) and flipping the ProviderEnableInfo bit on the ETW Threat-Intelligence provider, Lazarus can subsequently dump LSASS and run malware with zero EDR alerts. In the documented Zeek / Suricata NDR exchange from appid.sys (AppLocker Driver) to FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine, FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine responds with ALERT Host/NDR Gap (confirming that the KAOLIN RAT C2 request succeeded on FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky, Microsoft & Avast, Lazarus Group (Diamond Sleet): appid.sys Zero-Day & FUDModule Rootkit). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ KAOLIN RAT C2 / ⇠#3 ALERT Host/NDR Gap) from Node ③ (#3 appid.sys (AppLocker Driver)) to Node ④ (#4 FUDModule v3 DKOM Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysmon & Defender XDR Sensor).

## 25. Mandiant & CISA — APT29 (Midnight Blizzard): JetBrains TeamCity RCE & GraphicalProton
- **Scenario ID:** `mandiant-apt29-teamcity-jetstream`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/mandiant-apt29-teamcity-jetstream
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-42793 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT29 (Midnight Blizzard / Cozy Bear), Lazarus & Ransomware Post-Disclosure Exploiters
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The developer meant to exempt only the root /RPC2 path from login checks, but wrote /**/RPC2, accidentally exempting every URL in the entire server that ends with /RPC2. Requesting /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 tricks TeamCity into creating a new admin token named "RPC2" for User ID 1 without asking for a password. As detailed by SonarSource and Rapid7, in vulnerable TeamCity versions the RequestInterceptors authentication filter excluded any URL matching //RPC2 from login checks (intended only to exempt the legacy XML-RPC endpoint at /RPC2, but the leading "/" Ant-path wildcard accidentally exempted every URL on the server that ended with "/RPC2"). The attacker exploits this by sending an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 (where "id:1" targets the primary built-in Super-Administrator account, and the REST API interprets the trailing "/RPC2" simply as the name to give the new token, causing TeamCity to mint and return a full Super-Admin Bearer token in the HTTP 200 response without asking for a password). Because TeamCity’s REST API endpoint for creating access tokens follows the URL template /app/rest/users/{userLocator}/tokens/{tokenName}, naming the token "RPC2" satisfies both the REST controller parameter and the /**/RPC2 authentication-bypass wildcard simultaneously (CVE-2023-42793). In the documented TeamCity Access Log exchange from APT29 (Midnight Blizzard) to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP CVE-2023-42793 (confirming that the MINT RPC2 TOKEN request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 DEBUG PROCESS RCE & CI/CD SECRET HARVESTING). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ MINT RPC2 TOKEN / ⇠#1 RESP CVE-2023-42793) from Node ① (#1 APT29 (Midnight Blizzard)) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Holding the freshly minted Super-Admin token, the attacker flips on a hidden "Developer Debug Terminal" switch (rest.debug.processes.enable=true), runs their operating-system commands, and then immediately shreds the RPC2 token so admins checking the active token list see nothing. Authenticating with Authorization: Bearer <token>, the attacker first sets the internal server property rest.debug.processes.enable=true (unlocking a hidden administrative diagnostic feature that is disabled by default), and then sends POST requests to /app/rest/debug/processes?exePath=cmd.exe&params=/c+... (telling the TeamCity Java server to spawn arbitrary OS commands on the underlying host). Seconds later, the attacker sends DELETE /app/rest/users/id:1/tokens/RPC2 (erasing the "RPC2" token right after creating a stealthier backdoor so an administrator checking the active tokens page in the UI sees nothing suspicious). Although deleting the RPC2 token removes it from the current UI token table, the token creation and deletion events remain recorded in logs/teamcity-activities.log and child process creations are captured by endpoint telemetry. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD, JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD responds with ACK PID 6740 (confirming that the TEAMCITY DEBUG RCE request succeeded on JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 GRAPHICALPROTON IMPLANT & ONEDRIVE GRAPH API C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ TEAMCITY DEBUG RCE / ⇠#2 ACK PID 6740) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because the CI/CD build server is the automated assembly line that deploys software to every cloud and server in the company, taking over this one room hands the attacker the master keys to cloud deployments, source code, and code-signing certificates. Because a CI/CD build server is the central factory that compiles software and deploys it into production, it stores high-privilege secrets (AWS/Azure deployment keys, GitHub SSH keys, and Authenticode code-signing certificates). As documented by Mandiant and CISA, APT29 extracts TeamCity’s encryption keys (encryption-config.xml, allowing them to decrypt every stored cloud and database password in the CI/CD database), sideloads their GraphicalProton backdoor via DLL hijacking (using Microsoft OneDrive and Dropbox Graph APIs for encrypted C2), and pivots into Active Directory. Compromising a CI/CD server gives the attacker a force-multiplier: they can both steal production cloud credentials stored in build variables and inject malicious code into software packages being built and signed by the server. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 & 3 exchange from JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD to GraphicalProton Backdoor, GraphicalProton Backdoor responds with ACK OneDrive C2 (confirming that the GRAPHICALPROTON C2 request succeeded on GraphicalProton Backdoor and completing the final execution objective of Mandiant & CISA, APT29 (Midnight Blizzard): JetBrains TeamCity RCE & GraphicalProton). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ GRAPHICALPROTON C2 / ⇠#3 ACK OneDrive C2) from Node ③ (#3 JetBrains TeamCity CI/CD) to Node ④ (#4 GraphicalProton Backdoor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise SIEM & EDR).

  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Adding /anything after /SetupWizard.aspx fools the security filter into thinking you are visiting a different page, while ASP.NET treats /anything as harmless PathInfo metadata and opens the First-Time Setup Wizard anyway. In ASP.NET, a URL like /Page.aspx/extra is routed to the handler for /Page.aspx with Request.PathInfo set to "/extra". Because the security check tested Request.Path instead of Request.FilePath, a single trailing "/" bypassed the lock completely. ## 27. Andres Freund, Red Hat & Kaspersky — XZ Utils (liblzma) IFUNC sshd Supply Chain Backdoor
- **Scenario ID:** `xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/xz-utils-cve-2024-3094-backdoor
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-3094 (10.0 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Jia Tan (XZ Utils Maintainer Persona), Jigar Kumar / Dennis Ens Sockpuppet Cluster
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The malicious code is not visible in the normal C source files on GitHub; instead, a rigged build script (build-to-host.m4) unpacks a hidden binary object from a "corrupt test file" (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz) only when building release packages, and libsystemd carries that poisoned library straight into sshd. During package compilation of XZ Utils 5.6.0 and 5.6.1, a tampered macro file named build-to-host.m4 decodes hidden shell commands from two test archives, tests/files/bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz and tests/files/good-large_compressed.lzma (hidden inside binary test files so code reviewers inspecting C source files on GitHub would see nothing suspicious), and splices a precompiled backdoor object into liblzma_la-crc64-fast.o. On Debian, Fedora, Ubuntu, and RHEL systems, the OpenSSH server (/usr/sbin/sshd) is compiled with libsystemd.so.0 support (so sshd can notify systemd when the service is ready, which transitively loads /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/liblzma.so.5.6.1 directly into every sshd process). Why did Andres Freund catch this? Because parsing the symbol tables inside the backdoored liblzma.so.5.6.1 added ~500 milliseconds (~2.3 billion CPU cycles) to every failed SSH login, which Freund spotted while profiling Debian sid with perf. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LIBLZMA 5.6.1 LOAD / ⇠#1 ACK liblzma 5.6.1) from Node ① (#1 Jia Tan / APT Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Before sshd even runs its first line of code in main(), the Linux library loader asks liblzma which CRC64 math function fits the CPU best (IFUNC). The rigged resolver uses that early wakeup call to swap out OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt phone number in memory. When a program starts on Linux, the GNU dynamic linker (ld-linux-x86-64.so.2) resolves Indirect Functions (IFUNC, a legitimate glibc feature designed to let libraries pick the fastest CPU-specific math routine before main() even begins). When the linker calls crc64_resolve() inside liblzma.so.5.6.1, the injected _get_cpuid() function checks that argv[0] is "/usr/sbin/sshd" and that debugging variables like LD_DEBUG are not set, then hooks _dl_audit_preinit to overwrite the Global Offset Table (GOT) pointer for OpenSSL’s RSA_public_decrypt (redirecting every future RSA signature check inside sshd to the backdoor’s own function). By executing inside an IFUNC resolver during dynamic linking, the backdoor modifies the in-memory GOT pointer for RSA_public_decrypt before OpenSSH’s main() function or privilege-separation sandbox even initializes. In the documented ELF IFUNC Resolver exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Linux Server (sshd :22), Linux Server (sshd :22) responds with ACK +2.3B Cycles (confirming that the IFUNC GOT HOOK request succeeded on Linux Server (sshd :22) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 ED448 SSH CERTIFICATE VERIFICATION & PRE-AUTH SYSTEM() RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ IFUNC GOT HOOK / ⇠#2 ACK +2.3B Cycles) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Linux Server (sshd :22)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When the attacker connects over SSH, they hide an encrypted command inside the RSA public-key modulus (N) signed with their private Ed448 key. The hooked RSA_public_decrypt verifies the Ed448 signature and runs the command as root, while normal users’ SSH logins continue working normally! When the attacker connects to TCP port 22 and sends an SSH public-key authentication request (SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST), sshd calls the hooked RSA_public_decrypt() to verify the client’s key. The backdoor inspects the RSA modulus N for a magic arithmetic header (a*b + c <= 3), decrypts the embedded payload using ChaCha20, and verifies it against a hardcoded 32-byte Ed448 public key (ensuring that only the threat actor holding the matching Ed448 private key can trigger the backdoor, while all normal SSH connections pass straight through to the real RSA_public_decrypt). Once verified, the backdoor passes the decrypted command string to system() as root (UID 0). Because the hooked RSA_public_decrypt executes inside the privileged sshd monitor process before authentication completes, the command runs with full root privileges and leaves zero failed-login entries in /var/log/auth.log. In the documented Auditd SYSCALL 59 exchange from Linux Server (sshd :22) to liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook, liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the PRE-AUTH ROOT RCE request succeeded on liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook and completing the final execution objective of Andres Freund, Red Hat & Kaspersky, XZ Utils (liblzma) IFUNC sshd Supply Chain Backdoor). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PRE-AUTH ROOT RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 Linux Server (sshd :22)) to Node ④ (#4 liblzma IFUNC & GOT Hook), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & eBPF SIEM).

## 29. Qualys TRU & CISA — OpenSSH "regreSSHion": SIGALRM Async-Signal-Unsafe syslog() Heap RCE
- **Scenario ID:** `openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/openssh-regreSSHion-cve-2024-6387
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2024-6387 (8.1 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Opportunistic & APT Linux Infrastructure Operators, Cloud & Botnet Initial Access Brokers
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Before the 120-second LoginGraceTime stopwatch hits zero, the attacker sends a carefully choreographed sequence of SSH public-key packets so the server’s memory ledger (glibc main_arena) is lined up with alternating 4 KB and 320-byte slots. To prepare the memory layout inside the privileged pre-authentication sshd child process, the attacker opens concurrent TCP/22 connections and sends a series of SSH2_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST packets containing crafted RSA/certificate public keys (allocating and freeing specific chunk sizes so glibc’s heap allocator arranges alternating 4 KB and 320-byte holes right before the 120-second LoginGraceTime timer expires). Why is this vulnerability called "regreSSHion"? Because OpenSSH originally fixed this exact signal-handler race in 2006 (CVE-2006-5051) by adding #ifdef DO_LOG_SAFE_IN_SIGHAND to sigdie(), but an unrelated code cleanup in October 2020 (OpenSSH 8.5p1) accidentally deleted that #ifdef guard. In the documented sshd Auth.log Flood exchange from Remote Exploit Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ACK 120.000s Timeout (confirming that the LOGINGRACETIME STORM request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 SIGALRM INTERRUPTS FREE() & CALLS ASYNC-SIGNAL-UNSAFE SYSLOG()). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ LOGINGRACETIME STORM / ⇠#1 ACK 120.000s Timeout) from Node ① (#1 Remote Exploit Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker sends one final packet timed so that the 120-second SIGALRM bell rings while sshd is halfway through free(). The alarm handler calls syslog(), which calls fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320) on the half-updated heap pointers. The attacker times their final packet so that when the kernel delivers SIGALRM (signal 14, triggered when LoginGraceTime reaches 120 seconds), the main sshd thread is halfway through glibc’s _int_free() function (after modifying a heap chunk’s size metadata, but before updating the bin’s forward/backward pointers). The asynchronous signal handler grace_alarm_handler() calls sigdie("Timeout before authentication..."), which calls syslog() (an async-signal-unsafe C library function that internally calls __tzfile_read() -> fopen("/etc/localtime") -> malloc(320), causing glibc to allocate a 320-byte FILE structure overlapping the attacker’s packet buffer in memory). Why wasn’t OpenBSD vulnerable to CVE-2024-6387? Because OpenBSD’s syslog_r() implementation is explicitly designed to be async-signal-safe and never calls malloc() or fopen(), whereas Linux’s glibc syslog() dynamically allocates heap memory. In the documented SIGALRM / glibc Arena exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1), Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1) responds with ACK 320-Byte Overlap (confirming that the SYSLOG HEAP RACE request succeeded on Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 GLIBC _IO_FILE VTABLE HIJACK & PRE-AUTH ROOT CODE EXECUTION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SYSLOG HEAP RACE / ⇠#2 ACK 320-Byte Overlap) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because fopen("/etc/localtime") placed its 320-byte FILE control sheet right on top of the attacker’s buffer, the attacker overwrites the sheet’s function table (_IO_wfile_jumps) so that reading the timezone file executes /bin/sh as root. Because the 320-byte _IO_FILE structure allocated by fopen("/etc/localtime") sits inside memory controlled by the attacker’s SSH packet, the attacker crafts fake _wide_data and _vtable_offset fields pointing to glibc’s internal _IO_wfile_jumps vtable (redirecting the stream’s underflow function _IO_wfile_underflow to an arbitrary code pointer). The moment __tzfile_read() tries to read the timezone file via __uflow(), execution jumps into the attacker’s payload running inside the privileged pre-authentication sshd process (with full root UID 0 privileges, completely outside OpenSSH’s unprivileged network sandbox). Although winning the ASLR + timing race takes ~10,000 connections (roughly 3 to 6 hours against default MaxStartups), every failed attempt simply closes a child process while the master sshd daemon automatically forks fresh children. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ROOT VTABLE RCE / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ③ (#3 Linux OpenSSH Server (9.6p1)) to Node ④ (#4 SIGALRM -> syslog() Race), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Auth Log & Network SIEM).

Even after GitHub took down the IconStorages repository, the shellcode also contained a fallback list of hardcoded C2 domains disguised to look like Akamai, Azure, and Microsoft storage services. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ GITHUB .ICO DEAD-DROP / ⇠#2 ACK AES-GCM C2 URL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Workstation (3CX)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / Kaspersky EDR SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The C2 server sends back a memory-only thief (ICONICSTEALER) that raids Chrome, Edge, and Brave browser databases, and if the victim works at a cryptocurrency exchange, the operator sends in the heavy-duty Gopuram espionage backdoor. Connecting to the decrypted C2 URL with an encrypted "tutma=" cookie, the loader downloads and reflectively loads a third-stage DLL strictly in memory: ICONICSTEALER (an information stealer documented by Mandiant and CrowdStrike that enumerates the workstation and reads SQLite History and Login Data files from Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, and Mozilla Firefox). Furthermore, as Kaspersky GReAT uncovered, on high-value cryptocurrency and financial victims the threat actor deployed Gopuram (a sophisticated modular C2 backdoor used exclusively by the Lazarus group). Mandiant subsequently traced how the 3CX supply chain attack itself began: Lazarus had earlier trojanized the website installer for Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software, which an employee at 3CX downloaded, creating a supply-chain-to-supply-chain cascade. In the documented EDR Memory / File Access exchange from Enterprise Workstation (3CX) to ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll, ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll responds with ACK In-Memory DLL (confirming that the ICONICSTEALER & GOPURAM request succeeded on ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll and completing the final execution objective of CrowdStrike, Kaspersky & Mandiant, Lazarus (SmoothOperator): 3CXDesktopApp Supply Chain & Gopuram). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ICONICSTEALER & GOPURAM / ⇠#3 ACK In-Memory DLL) from Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Workstation (3CX)) to Node ④ (#4 ffmpeg.dll & d3dcompiler_47.dll), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / Kaspersky EDR SIEM).

## 32. Microsoft, CrowdStrike & Splunk — Active Directory "noPac": sAMAccountName Spoofing & KDC Impersonation
- **Scenario ID:** `nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/nopac-samaccountname-cve-2021-42278-42287
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2021-42287 (8.8 HIGH / CRITICAL AD EOP), CVE-2021-42278 (8.8 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Ransomware Affiliates & APT Lateral Movement Operators, Deep Instinct / Red Team Exploitation Clusters
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Using the default quota that lets any user add 10 computers to the domain (ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota = 10), the attacker creates FAKEPC01$, strips off the $ to rename it CORP-DC01, and asks the KDC for a Kerberos TGT. By default in Active Directory, the attribute ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota is set to 10 (meaning any standard domain user can create up to 10 new computer accounts over LDAP without needing administrator rights). The attacker creates a computer account named FAKEPC01$, and then exploits CVE-2021-42278 (an LDAP validation flaw where Active Directory forgot to enforce that a computer account’s sAMAccountName must end with a trailing "$" sign when modified) to rename the computer’s sAMAccountName to CORP-DC01, matching the exact hostname of the target Domain Controller, and requests a Kerberos TGT (EventID 4768). Why didn’t Active Directory block the rename as a duplicate name? Because the real Domain Controller’s sAMAccountName is "CORP-DC01$" (with a dollar sign), so "CORP-DC01" (without a dollar sign) is treated by LDAP as a distinct string. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ SPOOF DC SAMACCOUNTNAME / ⇠#1 ACK EID 4781) from Node ① (#1 Compromised Domain User) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): While holding the CORP-DC01 TGT in their hand, the attacker renames their fake computer back to FAKEPC01$ and asks the KDC for an S4U2self service ticket. When the KDC can’t find CORP-DC01, it automatically adds $ (CORP-DC01$) and issues a ticket for the real Domain Controller! Holding the valid TGT for "CORP-DC01", the attacker renames their machine account back to FAKEPC01$ over LDAP (so no account named "CORP-DC01" exists in Active Directory anymore) and sends a Kerberos S4U2self TGS request (KRB_TGS_REQ, asking the KDC to issue a service ticket impersonating the Domain Administrator to itself). When the KDC looks up the TGT’s client name ("CORP-DC01") and fails to find it, CVE-2021-42287 triggers: kdcsvc.dll automatically appends a trailing "$" ("CORP-DC01$") and searches again, matching the real Domain Controller and encrypting a Domain Admin service ticket with the real Domain Controller’s secret key! Why is CVE-2021-42287 so critical? Because the KDC validates the incoming TGT using the attacker’s key, but encrypts the outgoing S4U2self TGS ticket (and its high-privilege Domain Admin PAC) for the real Domain Controller ("CORP-DC01$"). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ KDC "$" FALLBACK TGS / ⇠#2 ACK EID 4769) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker walks up to the real Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) and hands over the freshly minted cifs/CORP-DC01 Domain Admin ticket, dumping every password hash in the company from NTDS.dit. Presenting the forged cifs/CORP-DC01.corp.local Kerberos service ticket (which carries a valid Privilege Attribute Certificate for the Domain Administrator signed by the KDC itself), the attacker authenticates to the Domain Controller and invokes the MS-DRSR directory replication protocol (DCSync, DrsGetNCChanges, which instructs the Domain Controller to replicate the NTLM and AES password hashes of krbtgt and all domain users from NTDS.dit). From start to finish, tools like noPac.exe and sam_the_admin.py complete all three steps automatically in under 3 seconds. In the documented WinSec EID 4662 (DCSync) exchange from Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) to KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine, KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine responds with ACK EID 4662 (confirming that the DCSYNC REPLICATION request succeeded on KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft, CrowdStrike & Splunk, Active Directory "noPac": sAMAccountName Spoofing & KDC Impersonation). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DCSYNC REPLICATION / ⇠#3 ACK EID 4662) from Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)) to Node ④ (#4 KDC S4U2self Ticket Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Splunk SIEM & Identity Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**

## 33. Secura, CISA & CrowdStrike — Active Directory "Zerologon": Netlogon AES-CFB8 All-Zero IV Takeover
- **Scenario ID:** `zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/zerologon-netlogon-cve-2020-1472
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2020-1472 (10.0 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT28, MuddyWater, Chimera & Ryuk/Conti Affiliates, Wizard Spider (Ryuk / Conti Ransomware)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because ComputeNetlogonCredential uses AES-CFB8 with an all-zero IV, sending 8 zero bytes as the ClientChallenge has a 1-in-256 chance of producing 8 zero bytes as the ClientCredential. In less than 3 seconds, one of the 256 tries hits the jackpot! As proven by Secura, in the Netlogon handshake (NetrServerReqChallenge followed by NetrServerAuthenticate3), the client proves it knows the machine password by encrypting an 8-byte ClientChallenge using ComputeNetlogonCredential(). However, Microsoft implemented this function using AES-CFB8 (8-bit Cipher Feedback mode, which encrypts 1 byte at a time by XORing each plaintext byte with the first byte of AES applied to a 16-byte sliding window) and hardcoded the 16-byte Initialization Vector (IV) to all zeroes (0x00*16, violating the fundamental rule of cryptography that an IV must be random). When the attacker sets ClientChallenge = 0x0000000000000000, there is a 1-in-256 probability that the first AES block starts with 0x00, causing all 8 encrypted bytes to stay 0x0000000000000000! Because Netlogon has no rate-limiting or account lockout on computer accounts, an unauthenticated attacker on the network can fire ~256 RPC attempts in under 3 seconds until the random session key happens to produce the all-zero output. In the documented System EID 5805 + Zeek RPC exchange from Internal Network Attacker to Core Identity & VLAN Switch, Core Identity & VLAN Switch responds with ACK 214 RPC Tries (confirming that the NRPC ZERO-IV BRUTE request succeeded on Core Identity & VLAN Switch and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 OVERWRITING THE DOMAIN CONTROLLER PASSWORD VIA NETRSERVERPASSWORDSET2). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ NRPC ZERO-IV BRUTE / ⇠#1 ACK 214 RPC Tries) from Node ① (#1 Internal Network Attacker) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Even though the attacker passed the front-door check, they still don’t know what random SessionKey the Domain Controller picked. So they uncheck the "Encrypt Our Conversation" box (Flags = 0x212fffff) and tell the Domain Controller (NetrServerPasswordSet2): "Change your own CORP-DC01$ password to blank!" During the NetrServerAuthenticate3 call, the attacker clears the Netlogon Sealing flag (NegotiateFlags = 0x212fffff, telling the Domain Controller not to require RPC packet encryption on this session, which was still allowed by default in 2020 for backwards compatibility) and then invokes NetrServerPasswordSet2 with a 516-byte buffer of all zeroes. Because encrypting 516 zero bytes with AES-CFB8 and an all-zero IV also produces all zeroes, the Domain Controller overwrites its own computer account password (CORP-DC01$) in Active Directory NTDS.dit with an empty password (NTLM hash 31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0). Because this RPC call runs over an unauthenticated network pipe rather than a logged-in user session, Windows logs Security EventID 4742 ("A computer account was modified") with SubjectUserName: ANONYMOUS LOGON. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DC$ PASSWORD WIPE / ⇠#2 ACK EID 4742) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now that CORP-DC01$ has a blank password in Active Directory, the attacker logs in as CORP-DC01$ with no password, downloads every password hash in the company via DCSync, and then puts the original password back from the DC’s local registry so nobody notices the DC broke! Because a Domain Controller’s computer account (CORP-DC01$) automatically belongs to the Enterprise Domain Controllers group, the attacker authenticates over SMB/RPC as CORP\CORP-DC01$ using the empty NTLM hash (31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0) and runs DCSync (DrsGetNCChanges, dumping the Domain Administrator and krbtgt hashes from NTDS.dit). Finally, because wiping CORP-DC01$’s password in AD causes it to go out of sync with the password stored in the DC’s local registry (HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC, which would break DNS and AD replication), the attacker uses their new Domain Admin credentials to read $MACHINE.ACC and restore the original machine password. Why did Zerologon break Domain Controllers when naive attackers forgot Step 3? Because NetrServerPasswordSet2 updates NTDS.dit without updating the DC’s local LSA secret ($MACHINE.ACC), locking the DC out of its own domain until restored. In the documented WinSec EID 4624 & 4662 exchange from Domain Controller (CORP-DC01) to Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset, Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset responds with ACK NTLM 31d6cfe0... (confirming that the DC$ EMPTY-HASH DCSYNC request succeeded on Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset and completing the final execution objective of Secura, CISA & CrowdStrike, Active Directory "Zerologon": Netlogon AES-CFB8 All-Zero IV Takeover). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ DC$ EMPTY-HASH DCSYNC / ⇠#3 ACK NTLM 31d6cfe0...) from Node ③ (#3 Domain Controller (CORP-DC01)) to Node ④ (#4 Netlogon AES-CFB8 & Password Reset), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CrowdStrike / SIEM Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Secura BV (Tom Tervoort) — *Zerologon: Unauthenticated Domain Controller Compromise by Subverting Netlogon Cryptography (CVE-2020-1472)* (`SECURA-ZEROLOGON-2020`): https://www.secura.com/blog/zero-logon
  - Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) — *Emergency Directive 20-04: Mitigate Netlogon Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability from August 2020 Patch Tuesday* (`CISA-ED-20-04`): https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-20-04-mitigate-netlogon-elevation-privilege-vulnerability-august-2020-patch
  - Microsoft Threat Intelligence & CrowdStrike — *Detecting CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon) via Windows EventID 5805, 4742 & Netlogon RPC Inspection* (`MS-DEFENDER-ZEROLOGON`): https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2020/09/28/new-detections-for-cve-2020-1472-active-exploitation/

## 34. DEVCORE, Mandiant & CISA — Microsoft Exchange "ProxyShell": Autodiscover SSRF to MailboxExport Webshell
- **Scenario ID:** `proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/proxyshell-exchange-cve-2021-34473
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2021-34473 (9.8 CRITICAL), CVE-2021-34523 (9.8 CRITICAL), CVE-2021-31207 (7.2 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Conti, LockBit, BlackByte & APT27 / Hafnium Clusters, FIN12 & LockFile Ransomware Operators
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Exchange’s RemoveExplicitLogonFromUrlAnchoredXml function tries to delete the email address from the URL, but a missing / check in its regex lets ?@foo.com trick it into deleting /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com, turning the URL into /powershell/! In Microsoft Exchange’s Architecture, the internet-facing Frontend Client Access Service (CAS on TCP 443) authenticates users and proxies their requests to the internal Backend server (on TCP 444) using Exchange’s own machine certificate (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM). As Orange Tsai discovered, when a URL starts with /autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com/powershell/, the frontend’s Explicit-Logon parser strips "/autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@foo.com" thinking it is an email address prefix, and proxies the remaining path, /powershell/, straight to the internal Backend server with full SYSTEM authentication (CVE-2021-34473, bypassing all frontend login checks). Attackers also used an alternate form discovered in the wild: placing the path inside an HTTP cookie (Cookie: Email=autodiscover/autodiscover.json%3F@foo.com) so simple URL filters looking for "@foo.com" in the URI query string would miss it. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ AUTODISCOVER PATH BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200) from Node ① (#1 ProxyShell Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When the proxied request arrives in the Backend /powershell/ room, the clerk says: "I see the building’s SYSTEM stamp, but which user am I running commands for?" The attacker hands over ?X-Rps-CAT=... containing the Exchange Administrator’s SID! When the proxied request reaches the Backend PowerShell endpoint (:444/powershell/), it initially fails because the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM computer account does not have a user security token attached. Exploiting CVE-2021-34523, the attacker appends the query parameter ?X-Rps-CAT=<Base64_CommonAccessToken> (a serialized Windows CommonAccessToken structure that the Backend PowerShell module trusts without signature verification, allowing the attacker to plug in the Exchange Administrator’s Security Identifier / SID and open a full administrative Exchange PowerShell session). Inside that session, the attacker runs New-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role "Mailbox Import Export" -User "admin@corp.local". How did the attacker know the Exchange Administrator’s SID before logging in? By first sending a quick autodiscover/mapi request through the same CVE-2021-34473 proxy to convert the administrator’s email address into their legacyExchangeDN and Windows SID. In the documented MSExchange Mgmt EID 1 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Exchange Server (CAS Frontend), Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) responds with ACK EID 1 Cmdlet (confirming that the MAILBOX EXPORT CMDLET request succeeded on Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 NEW-MAILBOXEXPORTREQUEST ARBITRARY .ASPX WEBSHELL WRITE (CVE-2021-31207)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MAILBOX EXPORT CMDLET / ⇠#2 ACK EID 1 Cmdlet) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Exchange Server (CAS Frontend)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Normally New-MailboxExportRequest saves a .pst email archive file. By hiding an ASPX webshell inside a draft email and telling Exchange to export that mailbox to \\127.0.0.1\c$\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\shell.aspx, IIS runs the email attachment as a live SYSTEM webshell! With the "Mailbox Import Export" role assigned, the attacker saves a draft email containing an encoded JScript/C# ASPX webshell, and then executes New-MailboxExportRequest -Mailbox admin@corp.local -FilePath "\\127.0.0.1\c$\inetpub\wwwroot\aspnet_client\shell.aspx" (CVE-2021-31207, abusing the Exchange Mailbox Replication service, which runs as SYSTEM, to write a file to any UNC path on the server). Even though the exported file is a binary .PST mailbox archive (starting with magic bytes !BDN), naming it .aspx causes IIS’s ASP.NET engine to ignore the binary PST header and execute the <script runat="server"> webshell inside it as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM! Why did the raw ASPX code have to be specially encoded inside the draft email? Because Exchange normally compresses or encodes email bodies inside a PST file; Orange Tsai used a custom UTF-7 / uncompressed attachment trick so the exact ASCII characters <%@ Page ... %> appeared intact inside the binary PST file. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 & 11 exchange from Exchange Server (CAS Frontend) to Exchange PowerShell Backend, Exchange PowerShell Backend responds with ACK SYSTEM Shell (confirming that the ASPX WEBSHELL EXEC request succeeded on Exchange PowerShell Backend and completing the final execution objective of DEVCORE, Mandiant & CISA, Microsoft Exchange "ProxyShell": Autodiscover SSRF to MailboxExport Webshell). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ ASPX WEBSHELL EXEC / ⇠#3 ACK SYSTEM Shell) from Node ③ (#3 Exchange Server (CAS Frontend)) to Node ④ (#4 Exchange PowerShell Backend), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & Exchange Audit Sensor).

  - DEVCORE Security Research (Orange Tsai) — *ProxyShell: A New Attack Surface on MS Exchange Part 3 (CVE-2021-34473, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-31207)* (`DEVCORE-PROXYSHELL-2021`): https://devco.re/blog/2021/08/06/a-new-attack-surface-on-ms-exchange-part-3-ProxyShell/
